# Section 3 — Routing, Transport & Storage: Deep Bug-Hunt Report

**Owner:** Taksh Shah
**Section:** 3 — Routing, Transport & Storage (`docs/testing/CODE_REVIEW_SECTIONS.md`)
**Date:** 2026-08-25
**Commit reviewed:** `28a76f6` (branch `main`, clean tree)
**Toolchain:** cargo 1.97.1 · Windows 11

---

## 1. What this document is

A defect inventory for Section 3 only — path selection, every physical transport adapter, internet gateway bridging, the network simulator and ML routing predictor, telemetry, and durable storage. Roughly 23,000 lines across `iris-core`'s `routing/`, `transport/`, `gateway/`, `sim/`, `observability/`, `error.rs`, plus the whole `iris-storage` crate and the section's benches, loom models and integration tests.

Nothing outside that boundary is reported. `message.rs` and `protocol/envelope.rs` were read as read-only reference (they belong to Section 2) and appear here only where Section 3 code depends on them in a way that creates a defect on **our** side of the line.

Every finding carries: what the problem is, why it is a problem, exactly where it lives (file and line), why it came to exist, what it causes in production, how to fix it, and what else must change or be re-verified alongside it.

## Headline — read this first

Three results dominate this report. Read these before the individual findings, because they determine what the rest of it means.

**First: on real Android hardware, the Wi-Fi transports appear unable to move a single byte, and BLE may not either.** Reading the Rust adapters against the Kotlin they actually call surfaced seven Critical contract mismatches — peer handles allocated from two different namespaces, beacons that are never actually advertised, an NDP data path with no responder, a send that reports success for a frame it only queued. Each would independently prevent delivery. They are invisible to the test suite because the simulated adapters implement the Rust side's assumption by construction, and they are masked at runtime because the Kotlin adapters return success unconditionally — including on a device with no Wi-Fi Direct hardware at all. See §15 and Tier 0 of §17. **A two-device bench test would confirm or refute all nine of these in minutes, and should happen before any of them is "fixed".**

**Second: most of Section 3 is not connected to a production code path at all.** Routing, DTN/PRoPHET, the gateway engine and the entire storage crate are constructed only in their own tests. That does not make their defects unreal — every one was verified against the source — but it does mean they cannot cause an outage today. It also means they will all activate simultaneously, in a single future wiring PR, in code nobody will be re-reading at that moment. §5 sets out exactly what is live and what is not, and every severity in this report has been adjusted against it.

**Third, and beneath both of the above: no transport can be reached at all in production, on any platform, because nothing ever calls `Transport::connect()`.** `deliver_outbound` goes straight from selecting a transport to calling `send()` — it never establishes a link first, and `connect()` has exactly one production-shaped call site in the entire workspace, and that one is inside a `#[cfg(test)]` block. BLE and Wi-Fi Aware/Direct's `send()` consequently return `NotConnected` on every call, because their per-peer connection tables are populated only inside `connect()`. On desktop it is worse: `InternetTransport` is constructed `Unavailable` and only `connect()` ever advances it, so the transport manager's own eligibility filter (`state() >= Available`) excludes it from selection entirely — it is never even a candidate. This is why so much of this report reads as "latent": the send path is severed one hop before most of it. See GAP-7 and §16.

These three results interact rather than simply stack: the parts of this section that are wired may not work (GAP-7, and the FFI-seam findings for the parts that do get a link), and the parts that would work if reached are not wired (§5). Fixing GAP-7 is a precondition for observing almost everything else in this document on a real device — until it lands, most of Section 3's behaviour, good or bad, is unreachable.

Tiers 0, 1, 3, and 4 have no ordering dependency on each other and can in principle run in parallel once Tier -1 is closed — the loop runs them sequentially anyway (see the loop file for why: single-threaded git history, one thing reviewable at a time). Tier 2 is gated separately because it changes security/correctness invariants (routing loop prevention, gateway trust, storage exhaustion bounds) and needs a human — not just tests — to sign off before the loop is allowed to touch it.

**Tier 0 status note (2026-08-26):** Tier -1 is complete, so the loop's own run order would normally start Tier 0 next. It is intentionally paused instead: Tier 0 is the FFI-seam work (BLE, Wi-Fi Direct, Wi-Fi Aware on Android) and per §17's "What done means, per tier" it can only reach `✅ code-fixed`, never `🟢 hardware-verified`, without a physical device. Two Android devices are needed (these are peer-to-peer protocols — one device can't prove end-to-end delivery). **Tiers 1, 4, and 3 do not depend on Tier 0 and can run in the meantime** once hardware arrives and Tier 0 work is underway, per the loop's stated run order (0 → 1 → 4 → 3) — or ahead of Tier 0 if the devices aren't ready yet, since none of them have a hardware dependency.

### What "done" means, per tier — read before trusting a ✅

- **Tier -1, Tier 1, Tier 2, Tier 4:** ✅ means the fix compiled, the targeted test(s) passed, and (where one exists) the specific regression test named in the finding's *Fix* field was added or updated. Fully verifiable in-repo.
- **Tier 0 (FFI seam):** the loop can reach ✅ (code correct against the documented contract, unit/sim-tested) but **cannot** reach 🟢 (hardware-verified) — no physical Android device is available to this process. Tier 0 findings stay at ✅ with an explicit "PENDING HARDWARE VERIFICATION" note until a human runs the two-device bench test in §17 Tier 0 and promotes them to 🟢 by hand.
- **Tier 3 (simulator/ML):** ✅ requires the existing test suite plus any new determinism/leakage test the finding specifies to pass. No hardware dependency.

## 2. The result that frames everything else

**The entire Section 3 test suite passes — 0 failures — on the commit reviewed.**

```
cargo test -p iris-core --test sim_scenarios --test ml_experiments --test obs_telemetry --test tokio_behavior   → ok
cargo test -p iris-storage                                                                                     → ok
bash engineering/tools/verify-loom.sh                                                                          → 5 passed
cargo build -p iris-core -p iris-storage --all-targets                                                         → clean, no warnings
```

Every defect in this report is therefore one the current suite **cannot catch**. That is not incidental — a distinct class of finding here is *the test that appears to provide coverage and does not*:

- All 14 PostgreSQL-backed storage tests silently no-op and report **pass** when `IRIS_PG_PASSWORD` is unset (TAK-1). The storage layer's entire safety surface — P0-never-evicted, quota, sealing, schema hardening — is unverified.
- The loom concurrency models check no Section 3 code at all (TAK-18).
- The test that claims to guard the transport-selection comparator registers one transport, so it performs zero comparisons (TAK-19).
- Several property tests assert tautologies (ROUT-28, ROUT-29, ROUT-30).

Read the report with that in mind: a green build is currently evidence of very little in this section.

## 3. How the review was carried out

Six independent auditors swept disjoint slices of the section in parallel, each reading every line of its files rather than sampling, and each diffing the code against the governing design documents (`docs/routing/*`, `docs/transports/*`, `docs/simulation/*`, `docs/intelligence/*`, `docs/implementation/*_DESIGN|*_VERIFICATION.md`, `docs/legal/SPECTRUM_CONSIDERATIONS.md`) and the prior review records in `engineering/memory/records/`. A spec that says X where the code does Y is treated as a first-class defect, not a documentation nit.

Each auditor then re-read its own output and discarded what it could not defend, and made a second pass hunting for what the first pass missed.

A separate adversarial pass then tried to **refute** every Critical and High finding by re-reading the cited code independently, running the greps itself, and — where the claim was mechanical — proving or disproving it with a scratch program. Findings that survived are marked **CONFIRMED**; findings whose severity was overstated were downgraded with the reason recorded; findings that did not survive were removed or reclassified. Verdicts appear on the findings themselves.

A cross-cutting pass then looked for patterns no single-file reviewer could see — the systemic findings (SYS-*), which are the ones most worth fixing as a class rather than one site at a time.

A third round applied the two lenses the first two structurally could not. One read every Rust adapter **against the Kotlin and Swift it actually calls** (§15) — a seam no test in the repo crosses, and the one that produced this review's most consequential findings. The other was a completeness critic (§16): given everything already found, *what class of defect has nobody looked for?* — then hunted in the gaps it identified. Its blind-spot list is published in full, including the classes it did not have time to pursue, because knowing where the review stops is part of the result.

Claims of the form "this is never called" were proved with repo-wide greps that included `iris-android`, `iris-ios` and `iris-desktop`, since a Section 3 trait may only have an implementor on the platform side. Arithmetic and comparator claims were checked by execution rather than by reasoning.

Hardware was not required: `transport/simulated.rs` and `sim/scenario.rs` exist to exercise this logic without radios. That turned out to be a finding in itself — see SIM-* and RF-42/43/44/45 on how far the simulator diverges from the transports it stands in for.

## 4. How to read a finding

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Severity** | Consequence if it fires in production, independent of likelihood. | ⬜ |
| **Confidence** | `Certain` = the cited line is unambiguous. `High` = defect is clear, exact trigger may vary. `Medium` = mechanism is real, reachability not fully established. | ⬜ |
| **Verdict** | Result of the adversarial pass, where one was run. | ⬜ |
| **Location** | `file.rs:line` — line numbers are against commit `28a76f6`. | ⬜ |
| **Root cause** | Why the code came to be this way. Included because several defects here are the *same mistake repeated*, and those are only fixable at the cause. | ⬜ |
| **Dependencies / blast radius** | What else must change or be re-verified. Several fixes cross into Sections 2, 4 and 5 and need their owners' agreement — those are called out explicitly. | ⬜ |

### Severity scale

- **Critical** — remote denial of service, silent loss of P0/SOS traffic, a security control that does not hold, or a crash on a normal code path.
- **High** — message loss, a hang, unbounded resource growth, a documented requirement that is unimplemented, or regulatory exposure.
- **Medium** — degraded delivery, wrong-but-recoverable behaviour, unwired logic that will fire once connected, or a test that conceals a real defect.
- **Low** — diagnosability, hygiene, latent defects in code with no live caller.

### A note on "unwired" findings

A recurring category is code that is **defined, looks load-bearing, and is never called**. The routing engine (`RoutingEngine`), the gateway engine (`GatewayManager`), the battery cost model, `RadioConflictGroup`, the LoRa link-budget model and several config structs are all in this state. These are reported as defects rather than as future work for a specific reason: **each one will fire the moment it is wired up**, and the wiring commit is exactly the commit at which nobody will be re-reading this code. They are cheapest to fix now, while the defect is inert. Where a finding is latent for this reason, its severity reflects the latency and the entry says so.

---
## 5. Wiring status — which of these findings can bite today

This is the single most important structural result of the review, and it should be read before any individual finding.

**Most of Section 3 is not connected to a production code path.** The adversarial pass established this independently for two areas, and I then verified it across the whole section by tracing every engine from its definition to a real construction site in the platform crates (`crates/iris-android/src/engine.rs`, `crates/iris-ios/src/engine.rs`, `crates/iris-desktop/src/engine_handle.rs`).

| Component | Android | iOS | Desktop | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `TransportManager` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | **LIVE** |
| `BleTransport` (+ `ble_att`, `ble_advert`) | ✅ | ✅ | — | **LIVE** |
| `WifiAwareTransport` (+ beacon) | ✅ | — | — | **LIVE** |
| `WifiDirectTransport` (+ `wifi_direct_serv`) | ✅ | — | — | **LIVE** |
| `InternetTransport` | — | — | ✅ (relay) | **LIVE** |
| `transport/mod.rs`, `error.rs` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | **LIVE** |
| `LoRaTransport` | — | — | — | latent |
| `SatelliteTransport` | — | — | — | latent |
| `RoutingEngine`, `flood`, `direct`, `known_path`, `dedup_cache` | — | — | — | latent |
| `ScfEngine`, `prophet`, `scf_contact`, `scf_eviction`, `opportunistic` | — | — | — | latent |
| `GatewayManager` | — | — | — | latent |
| `PgStorage` / the whole `iris-storage` crate | — | — | — | latent |
| `sim/`, `sim/ml/` | — | — | — | simulation only, by design |

All three platforms construct the engine with `MemoryStorage`, not `PgStorage`:

```
iris-android/src/engine.rs:126   Arc::new(MemoryStorage::new()),
iris-ios/src/engine.rs:104       Arc::new(MemoryStorage::new()),
iris-desktop/src/engine_handle.rs:151   // D9: STORE-001 seam — MemoryStorage by default; PgStorage later.
iris-desktop/src/engine_handle.rs:153   Arc::new(MemoryStorage::new());
```

Only `iris-desktop` even declares a dependency on `iris-storage`, and it does not use it.

### What this changes

**It changes severities, not validity.** Every defect in this report is a real defect in real code — the adversarial pass found **no fabricated findings and no incorrect line citations**. But a defect on a path nothing executes cannot cause an outage today, and a report that labels fifteen such defects "Critical" will be dismissed wholesale. Severities throughout this document have therefore been corrected to reflect reachability, and each affected entry carries a **Verdict** line recording the downgrade and the reason. The pattern was consistent enough to name: *the most common error in the first pass was asserting production impact without first grepping for a production caller.*

**It does not make these findings low-priority.** It makes them **cheap**, and it puts them on a deadline:

1. **The wiring commit is the dangerous one.** Routing, DTN, gateway and storage will each be connected in a single future PR. That PR will be reviewed for *wiring* correctness, not for the latent defects it activates. Everything in Areas A, B, E-gateway and G fires at that moment, all at once, in code nobody is re-reading. Fixing them now costs a few hours; fixing them then means debugging a mesh that has just started misbehaving for fifteen simultaneous reasons.
2. **Two of these will bite on the wiring commit specifically.** SYS-1 (the `Instant` underflow) is inert only because `RoutingEngine::prune()` has no caller — and ROUT-11's recommended fix is to *give it one*. TAK-2 (unevictable P0 storage exhaustion) is inert only because `PgStorage` is unused. Both convert from "latent" to "live" as a direct consequence of the change that is coming.
3. **The live surface has its own serious problems.** The transports that *are* wired — BLE, Wi-Fi Aware, Wi-Fi Direct, internet — carry SYS-2 (no timeout on any adapter call), SYS-3 (silent inbound message loss with an unread counter), SYS-5 (poisoned-mutex amplification), and the per-adapter disconnect-handling defects in Area C. **These are live today and should be triaged first.**

### Reading guide

- Findings marked **LIVE** are in code that runs on a device now. Start here.
- Findings marked **latent** are real but unreachable today. They are gates on the wiring PR, not incident response. The correct action is to attach them to that PR as blocking review items.
- A handful are live in **CI rather than on-device** — most importantly TAK-1, where fourteen storage tests report success without running. That one is live right now, on every build.

## 6. Systemic findings — patterns that span the whole section

These four are not individual defects but *habits* visible only when the whole section is read at once. Each one is the reason several of the per-area findings below exist, and each is far cheaper to fix as a class — with a lint or a CI check — than one site at a time. Two of them (SYS-1, SYS-3) are cases where the team **already identified and fixed the problem once**, and the fix was scoped to the site where the symptom appeared rather than to the class. That pattern is the single most actionable observation in this report: without a mechanical guard, these will recur a third time.

#### SYS-1: A known, documented, already-fixed panic class was left unfixed at three routing sites
- **Severity:** Medium today — **High the moment the routing engine is wired up** (see ROUT-11)
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed  ·  Tier 1  ·  commit 4b03ae8  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain (the three sites and the prior fix) / verified as to reachability
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED, downgraded from Critical during adversarial verification. Two corrections were forced and are reflected below: the underflow is **platform-dependent** (it panics on Linux/Android; an empirical probe on Windows/rustc 1.97.1 did not), and `RoutingEngine::prune()` has **zero callers**, so the worst of the three sites cannot fire today. The systemic point — a documented, previously-fixed bug class left unfixed at three sites — is unaffected and is why this remains a headline finding.
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/dedup_cache.rs:63` (`evict_old`), `crates/iris-core/src/routing/known_path.rs:78` (`prune_expired`), `crates/iris-core/src/routing/mod.rs:301` (`prune`). Prior fix and incident record: `crates/iris-core/src/discovery/neighbor_table.rs:235-245` (`sweep`).
- **What:** `Instant::now() - duration` panics on underflow. `Instant` is monotonic-since-boot, so the subtraction underflows whenever process uptime is less than the duration being subtracted. The team hit this exact bug before, fixed it in `neighbor_table.rs`, and wrote a detailed comment explaining the failure mode — but three sites in `routing/` still use the anti-pattern the comment warns against.
- **Evidence:** The fix, with the incident recorded verbatim in the source:
```
neighbor_table.rs:236    // Compare elapsed-since-last-seen rather than building a cutoff
neighbor_table.rs:237    // instant. `Instant::now() - ttl` overflows and PANICS when process
neighbor_table.rs:238    // uptime is below the TTL — which is the normal case for an app that
neighbor_table.rs:239    // autostarts at device boot with the 300 s default. The panic happened
neighbor_table.rs:240    // inside the spawned discovery loop, so the task died silently and
neighbor_table.rs:241    // neighbour discovery stayed dead for the whole process lifetime.
neighbor_table.rs:244        .filter(|(_, n)| now.duration_since(n.last_seen) >= self.ttl)
```
  The three sites that were never updated:
```
dedup_cache.rs:63        let cutoff = Instant::now() - EXACT_WINDOW;
known_path.rs:78         let cutoff = Instant::now() - expiry;
mod.rs:301               let cutoff = Instant::now() - Duration::from_secs(3600);
```
  Repo-wide scan of Section 3 finds exactly these three occurrences of the pattern and no others.
- **Why it is wrong:** This is not a theoretical edge case — the source comment states it already happened in production and describes the consequence precisely, including that the failure was silent. The three surviving sites use windows of one hour (`dedup_cache.rs:63`, `mod.rs:301`) and the routing-table TTL (`known_path.rs:78`, 600 s default), so on Linux/Android each one is a live panic for the first hour (or ten minutes) after boot — precisely the window in which an app that autostarts at device boot does its work.

  Verification narrowed this in two important ways, and the honest framing matters more than the headline:
  - **Platform.** The underflow panics on Linux/Android. An empirical probe on Windows with rustc 1.97.1 did **not** panic, so this is invisible on the development host and only appears on the deployment target — which is worse, not better, for the odds of it being caught.
  - **Reachability today.** `RoutingEngine::prune()` has **zero callers** anywhere in the repo, including tests, so `mod.rs:301` cannot fire. `known_path::prune_expired` is called only from that dead `prune()` and from a unit test that passes 10 ms (too small to underflow). `dedup_cache::evict_old` is reachable today only through `sim/mod.rs:377` and `tests/protocol_conformance.rs:356`.

  So the correct claim is not "the node crashes on boot" — it is that **three loaded guns are sitting in code that is about to be wired up**, in a codebase that has already been shot by this exact bug once.
- **Root cause:** The fix was applied where the crash was observed rather than to the whole class. No lint, no CI grep, and no shared helper was introduced afterwards, so the remaining three sites had nothing to catch them. This is the same scoped-to-the-symptom remediation pattern seen in TAK-8 (`total_cmp` applied to two of five comparators).
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** *Today:* a simulator run or `protocol_conformance` test on a Linux/Android host with less than one hour of uptime hits `dedup_cache::evict_old` and panics with "overflow when subtracting duration from instant". *On the wiring commit:* the moment `RoutingEngine::prune()` gains a caller (ROUT-11 recommends exactly that, since without it the routing table and contact log grow unbounded), an Android device that reboots and autostarts IRIS panics inside whatever task calls it. Per the `neighbor_table.rs` incident note, if that is a spawned task the task dies silently and the subsystem stays dead for the whole process lifetime — no restart, no error surfaced.
- **Impact:** Today: spurious CI/simulator failures that look like flakes and will be attributed to the harness rather than to a real defect. On the wiring commit: silent, permanent death of routing-table pruning and dedup-cache eviction on every boot — and because pruning is what bounds those structures, the follow-on is unbounded memory growth in the routing table and contact log (compounding ROUT-11 and ROUT-13) on the low-memory devices this project targets. The reason to fix it now rather than then is that the wiring commit is exactly the commit at which nobody will be re-reading this code.
- **Fix:** Apply the `neighbor_table.rs` pattern at all three sites — compare elapsed time instead of constructing a cutoff instant:
```rust
// dedup_cache.rs:63
let now = Instant::now();
while let Some(front) = self.ring.front() {
    if now.duration_since(front.1) > EXACT_WINDOW { /* evict */ } else { break; }
}
// known_path.rs:78
let now = Instant::now();
self.entries.retain(|_, e| now.duration_since(e.last_confirmed) < expiry);
// mod.rs:301
let now = Instant::now();
self.contact_log.retain(|_, t| now.duration_since(*t) < Duration::from_secs(3600));
```
  Then prevent recurrence: add a CI grep (or a `clippy.toml` disallowed-method entry) rejecting `Instant::now() -` anywhere in the workspace. Without that, this will return a third time.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** Self-contained per site, but it should land as one change with the CI guard. Note that `RoutingEngine::prune()` currently has no production caller (ROUT-11), which masks the `mod.rs:301` instance today — fix this **before** wiring `prune()` up, or wiring it will introduce a boot-time crash.

#### SYS-2: Five of the six transports have no timeout on any adapter call — a hung radio blocks the node indefinitely
- **Severity:** High
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed  ·  Tier 1  ·  commit fec08ac  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** Production code in `crates/iris-core/src/transport/{ble,lora,satellite,wifiaware,wifi_direct}.rs` — no timeout anywhere. Only `crates/iris-core/src/transport/internet.rs:267,291,302` bounds its I/O.
- **What:** `tokio::time::timeout` appears 23 times across Section 3's transports, but 20 of those are inside `#[cfg(test)]` modules. Only three are production, all in `internet.rs`. Every call into a platform radio adapter — connect, send, scan, MTU negotiation, teardown — is awaited with no deadline.
- **Evidence:** Test-module boundaries established by `grep -n "^#\[cfg(test)\]"`:
```
ble.rs:906   lora.rs:1624   satellite.rs:1287   wifiaware.rs:1110
wifi_direct.rs:1332   simulated.rs:226   internet.rs:474
```
  Every `tokio::time::timeout` hit in those five radio files has a line number ABOVE its file's test-module start (ble 959–1735, lora 2330, satellite 1719, wifiaware 1180, wifi_direct 1416) — i.e. all are tests. The only production uses are:
```
internet.rs:267   match tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(3), TcpStream::connect(addr)).await {
internet.rs:291       tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(10), read.read_exact(&mut header))
internet.rs:302       tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(10), read.read_exact(&mut payload))
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `TransportError` defines `DiscoveryTimeout` and `ConnectionFailed` (`error.rs:14,20`), and the state machine defines a `Connecting` state — all of which presuppose that a stalled operation is eventually abandoned. Nothing can produce those errors from an actual hang. The abstraction promises bounded operations that the implementations do not deliver.
- **Root cause:** Each adapter was developed against its simulated coordinator, which always responds promptly, so a hang never appeared in any test. The timeouts written into the test bodies show the authors reached for deadlines when *observing* the system but not when *building* it.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A BLE peer moves out of range mid-GATT-connect. The Android `connectGatt` callback never fires. `BleTransport::connect` awaits forever. Because outbound delivery is sequential, the entire outbound queue — including P0 SOS — stalls behind it, with the transport still reporting `Connecting` so the manager keeps considering it viable. There is no watchdog anywhere to break the deadlock.
- **Impact:** A single unresponsive radio peer can silently and permanently stop all outbound traffic on the node. This is the highest-consequence failure mode in an emergency-communication system, and it is reachable without any attacker — ordinary radio behaviour produces it.
- **Fix:** Wrap every adapter call in a deadline and map the expiry onto the errors that already exist:
```rust
match tokio::time::timeout(CONNECT_TIMEOUT, self.adapter.connect(&addr)).await {
    Ok(r)  => r?,
    Err(_) => { self.state.store(TransportState::Available); return Err(TransportError::ConnectionFailed); }
}
```
  Add per-operation constants to each transport (connect / scan / send / teardown), sized from the radio's own characteristics. The timeout must also reset the state machine, or the transport strands itself in `Connecting` (see MG-2, which shows `Connecting` passes the eligibility filter).
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** Touches all five radio transports and the Android/iOS FFI adapters in Sections 4 & 5 (a timeout on the Rust side must not leave the native side still holding a callback). Fix alongside MG-2 (`Connecting` eligibility) and MG-5 (no failover), since a timeout is only useful if the manager then picks a different transport.

#### SYS-3: The inbound-lag counter — whose own comment says this failure "must never be invisible" — has no reader
- **Severity:** High
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (step 1)  ·  Tier 1  ·  commit 57f8d85  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/mod.rs:294-332` (`broadcast_stream`, `INBOUND_LAGGED_TOTAL`, `inbound_lagged_total`)
- **What:** Every transport publishes inbound messages through `broadcast::channel(1024)`. A `broadcast` channel drops the oldest items when a consumer falls behind. The helper correctly detects this and increments a counter — but `inbound_lagged_total()` has **zero callers repo-wide**, so the count is never exported, logged as a metric, alerted on, or used to trigger retransmission.
- **Evidence:** The stated intent, and the dead accessor:
```
mod.rs:300   /// A `Lagged` means inbound messages were dropped because the consumer fell
mod.rs:301   /// behind the channel. This used to `continue` silently, discarding the skipped
mod.rs:302   /// count — so a burst could drop traffic, including P0 SOS, with no metric, no
mod.rs:303   /// log and no retransmit trigger. In a disruption-tolerant mesh that is exactly
mod.rs:304   /// the failure that must never be invisible.
mod.rs:329   pub fn inbound_lagged_total() -> u64 {
mod.rs:330       INBOUND_LAGGED_TOTAL.load(std::sync::atomic::Ordering::Relaxed)
mod.rs:331   }
```
  `grep -rn "inbound_lagged_total" crates/ --include=*.rs` returns exactly one line: the definition at `mod.rs:330`. No caller, no test, no metric registration.
- **Why it is wrong:** The remediation added a `tracing::warn!` and a counter, then stopped short of exporting either. A `warn!` line in a log file is not a metric — nothing aggregates it, nothing alerts on it, and on a mobile device the log is usually discarded. The module's own stated goal ("must never be invisible") is therefore not met: the drop is *slightly* less invisible than before, but still not observable by any system that could react.
- **Root cause:** The fix was written to the letter of "add a counter" without the follow-through of wiring it into `observability/mod.rs` where the other metrics live. It is the same pattern as ROUT-27 (`iris.routing.floods_total` registered but never incremented) — metrics defined at one end and never connected at the other.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A node receives a burst of more than 1024 inbound frames faster than the engine drains them — entirely plausible during a flood, a reconnection backlog, or a deliberate flood attack. The oldest frames are dropped. If a P0 SOS was among them it is gone: no retransmission is triggered because nothing observes the loss. The only trace is a `warn!` line nobody reads.
- **Impact:** Silent P0/SOS message loss under exactly the burst conditions an emergency mesh is built for, with no operational signal that it occurred. Also blinds capacity planning — there is no way to know whether 1024 is the right channel depth because the overrun rate is unmeasured.

  **This is the milder half of the problem.** `broadcast_stream` is the *correct* consumer, and it is used for transport-level streams. The user-facing inbox does not go through it: all three platforms consume the engine's delivered-message channel with `while let Ok(env) = rx.recv().await` (`iris-android/src/engine.rs:213`, `iris-ios/src/engine.rs:193`, `iris-desktop/src/engine_handle.rs:282`). `Lagged` is an `Err`, so that loop does not skip the lost messages — it **exits**, permanently ending the forwarding task. One burst and the user's inbox stops delivering anything, for the life of the process, with no error surfaced. See GAP-4, where this is written up in full; it is a live defect on every platform.
- **Fix:** Register the counter as a real metric and split it per transport (today one global static is shared by both the state stream and the message stream of every transport — see MG-22, so a lagged *state* stream is indistinguishable from lost *messages*):
```rust
// in observability/mod.rs, alongside the existing counters
pub const TRANSPORT_INBOUND_LAGGED: &str = "iris.transport.inbound_lagged_total";
// and make broadcast_stream take a TransportId, incrementing a per-transport counter
```
  Then have the engine treat a non-zero delta as a signal to request retransmission, which is the part the doc comment promises and no code delivers.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `broadcast_stream` is called by all six transports, so adding a `TransportId` parameter touches each of them. Coordinate with `observability/mod.rs` (metric registration) and Section 2's engine (retransmit trigger). Fix together with MG-22.

#### SYS-4: Error-discarding `let _ =` is used 68 times across Section 3, concentrated in the gateway
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed  ·  Tier 1  ·  commit 5d3199c  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/gateway/mod.rs` and 13 other files — 68 occurrences across Section 3. Distribution: `gateway/mod.rs` 20, `wifiaware.rs` 9, `wifi_direct.rs` 8, `satellite.rs` 8, `lora.rs` 4, `internet.rs` 3, `ble.rs` 3, `opportunistic.rs` 3, `simulated.rs` 2, `manager.rs` 2, `sim/mod.rs` 2, `flood.rs` 2, `pg.rs` 1, `ble_att.rs` 1.
- **What:** `let _ = expr;` discards a `Result` without inspecting it. Used deliberately it is fine (e.g. a broadcast send with no subscribers legitimately fails). Used reflexively it erases the distinction between "expected no-op" and "the operation failed and the caller needed to know". At 68 sites there is no way to tell which is which by reading, and the per-adapter reviews found concrete cases in each category.
- **Evidence:** Counts from `grep -rc "let _ = "` over Section 3 source. The concentration in `gateway/mod.rs` (20 in 1281 lines — roughly one every 64 lines) is the outlier, and it sits in the module whose per-file review already flagged that every `TopologyEvent` it produces is discarded (MG-31).
- **Why it is wrong:** The section brief asks specifically whether "errors from the underlying OS API are surfaced or silently swallowed" for each adapter. This is the mechanical form of the answer: the codebase's default posture is to discard. Individual per-adapter findings (BLE-7 `set_mtu`, RF-17 `close()`, RF-27, MG-31) are instances of one systemic habit, and fixing them one at a time will not stop new ones appearing.
- **Root cause:** `let _ =` is the path of least resistance for satisfying `#[must_use]` on `Result`. Without a lint distinguishing intentional from accidental discards, the two are written identically.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** An adapter call fails — an MTU negotiation is rejected, a group teardown errors, a state event fails to publish. The caller proceeds as though it succeeded. The resulting misbehaviour surfaces much later and far away, with no log line connecting it to the discarded error.
- **Impact:** Diagnosis of field failures becomes guesswork, and genuine faults are converted into silent misbehaviour. No single instance is severe; the aggregate is why several of the per-adapter findings in this report are "cannot detect X" rather than "handles X incorrectly".
- **Fix:** Make the intent explicit and lintable. Enable `#![warn(unused_results)]` (or clippy's `let_underscore_must_use`) for these crates, then convert every intentional discard to a documented form:
```rust
// intentional: no subscribers is normal
let _: Result<_, _> = tx.send(event);   // broadcast with no receivers — expected
// unintentional: must be handled
self.adapter.set_mtu(peer, mtu).map_err(to_transport_err)?;
```
  Audit the 20 gateway sites first — that is where the density and the known consequences are highest.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** Enabling the lint will surface warnings across the whole crate; do it as a dedicated pass, not folded into a functional change. Individual fixes interact with BLE-7, RF-17, RF-27, and MG-31, which should be closed as part of this sweep.

#### SYS-5: 113 production `.lock().unwrap()` sites make every radio transport one panic away from permanently dead
- **Severity:** High
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (step 1)  ·  Tier 1  ·  commit 5b1422c  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain (mechanism) / Medium (ease of trigger)
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/{ble,wifiaware,wifi_direct,lora,satellite}.rs` — production code only (above each file's `#[cfg(test)]` boundary): `wifi_direct.rs` 35 sites, `ble.rs` 27, `wifiaware.rs` 27, `lora.rs` 13, `satellite.rs` 11. `internet.rs` and `simulated.rs` have none — they use tokio async locks throughout.
- **What:** These five transports hold their live state (`adapter`, `connections`, `scan_handle`, `adv_handle`, `pollers`, `scan_times`, session and peer maps) in `std::sync::Mutex`/`RwLock` and access it with `.lock().unwrap()`. A `std::sync::Mutex` becomes **poisoned** if any thread panics while holding its guard, and from that moment every `lock()` returns `Err`. With `.unwrap()` at all 113 sites, the first panic inside any lock scope converts that transport into a component that panics on every subsequent operation for the rest of the process lifetime.
- **Evidence:** Counts measured per file against each file's own test-module boundary:
```
ble.rs         : 27 production sites (test module starts line 906)
wifiaware.rs   : 27 production sites (test module starts line 1110)
wifi_direct.rs : 35 production sites (test module starts line 1332)
lora.rs        : 13 production sites (test module starts line 1624)
satellite.rs   : 11 production sites (test module starts line 1287)
internet.rs    :  0            simulated.rs   :  0
```
  The production state these guard, e.g.:
```
ble.rs:344   adapter: std::sync::Mutex<Option<std::sync::Arc<dyn BleAdapter>>>,
ble.rs:348   scan_handle: std::sync::Mutex<Option<ScanHandle>>,
ble.rs:353   connections: std::sync::Mutex<std::collections::HashMap<PeerId, (GattHandle, u16)>>,
ble.rs:356   pollers: std::sync::RwLock<std::collections::HashMap<PeerId, tokio::task::AbortHandle>>,
```
  There is no recovery path anywhere: `grep -rn "into_inner|is_poisoned" crates/iris-core/src/transport/` finds nothing.
- **Why it is wrong:** Two distinct problems. (1) **Amplification** — poisoning turns any single localised panic into a permanent whole-transport outage. The correct posture for a resilience-focused system is that a panic while handling one peer costs that peer, not the radio. (2) **Wrong primitive** — `std::sync::Mutex` in async code either blocks the executor thread or forces the guard to be dropped before every `.await`; the BLE review (BLE-2) found `connect()` already holding one across blocking FFI calls inside an `async fn`. The two transports that use tokio locks have neither problem, so the codebase already contains the correct pattern; it simply was not applied uniformly.
- **Root cause:** These adapters were built around synchronous FFI callbacks arriving on platform threads, where `std::sync::Mutex` is the natural choice, and the async layer was added over the top without revisiting the primitive. `.unwrap()` then followed as the idiomatic way to discharge the `LockResult`, on the assumption that poisoning cannot happen in code that does not panic.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Any panic inside any lock scope in these files — most plausibly an arithmetic or slicing panic while processing a malformed frame under the `connections` lock, or a panic propagated from a platform callback thread. The per-adapter review found no *directly* reachable panic from radio input in the BLE/Wi-Fi Aware files, which is why trigger confidence is Medium rather than High. But SYS-1 shows panics of exactly this kind already occur in this codebase, and one landing inside a lock scope is a matter of time.
- **Impact:** A single recoverable fault escalates to permanent loss of a radio for the process lifetime, with no self-healing and no error surfaced — the node simply stops using that transport. On a device where BLE is the only link, that is total isolation.
- **Fix:** Two steps, in order. (1) Remove the amplification cheaply — none of this state has an invariant a panic could have corrupted, so recovering from poisoning is safe:
```rust
#[inline]
fn lock_or_recover<T>(m: &std::sync::Mutex<T>) -> std::sync::MutexGuard<'_, T> {
    m.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())
}
```
  (2) Then migrate the state genuinely accessed from async contexts to `tokio::sync::Mutex`, which has no poisoning concept at all, matching `internet.rs`. Step 1 is mechanical and low-risk and can land immediately; step 2 is the real fix and should be scheduled per transport.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** Step 2 changes call sites from `.lock()` to `.lock().await`, forcing surrounding functions to become async, which may ripple into the FFI adapter traits in Sections 4 & 5 — a tokio lock cannot be taken from a synchronous platform callback, so those paths need a channel instead. Do BLE first, since BLE-2 already requires touching that code. Interacts with SYS-1 (fewer panics means less poisoning).

#### SYS-6: Mock transports that silently report success are `pub` in the production API
- **Severity:** Low
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed  ·  Tier 1  ·  commit ec2036d  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:179-181` (`SimulatedBleAdapter`), `crates/iris-core/src/transport/manager.rs:228-331` (`StubTransport`), `crates/iris-core/src/transport/simulated.rs` (whole module)
- **What:** Test doubles are declared `pub` and are not `#[cfg(test)]`-gated, so they compile into release builds and are reachable by any consumer of the crate. `StubTransport` in particular reports `send()` success without delivering anything (MG-18).
- **Evidence:**
```
ble.rs:179   /// In-memory BLE adapter for tests and simulation. No hardware involved.
ble.rs:180   #[derive(Default)]
ble.rs:181   pub struct SimulatedBleAdapter {
```
  No `#[cfg(test)]` or feature gate precedes it; the file's own test module does not begin until line 906.
- **Why it is wrong:** There is a legitimate reason for `SimulatedTransport` and `SimulatedBleAdapter` to be public — the section brief explicitly relies on them to exercise routing without hardware, and `iris-desktop` and the integration tests need them across crate boundaries. That argument does **not** extend to a type that reports success while discarding messages. A silent blackhole in the public API is one mistaken registration away from a node that appears healthy and delivers nothing.
- **Root cause:** Cross-crate test support cannot use `#[cfg(test)]` (it applies only to the defining crate's own test build), so the gate was dropped entirely rather than replaced with a feature flag.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** An integrator wiring up a new platform registers `StubTransport` as a placeholder during bring-up and forgets to replace it. Every send returns `Ok`, metrics show 100 % success, and no message is ever transmitted. Nothing in the manager distinguishes it from a real transport.
- **Impact:** Low today — no production caller registers them — but the failure mode (silent total message loss that presents as perfect health) is severe enough that the gate is worth restoring before it can happen.
- **Fix:** Put cross-crate test doubles behind a Cargo feature rather than leaving them ungated:
```toml
[features]
test-support = []
```
```rust
#[cfg(feature = "test-support")]
pub struct SimulatedBleAdapter { /* ... */ }
```
  Add `iris-core = { path = "…", features = ["test-support"] }` to the `[dev-dependencies]` of the crates that need it. `StubTransport` should additionally be deleted, or made to return `TransportError::NotSupported`, so that even when the feature is enabled it cannot silently swallow traffic.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** Touches `Cargo.toml` for `iris-core`, `iris-storage` and `iris-desktop`, plus the integration tests that construct these types. Coordinate with MG-18, which recommends the same treatment for `StubTransport`.

plus `crates/iris-core/benches/routing.rs`.

`docs/implementation/{ROUTE_VERIFICATION,ROUTE2_DESIGN,ROUTE2_VERIFICATION}.md`.

#### ROUT-1: `ForwardedCache::evict_old` panics on `Instant::now() - 1h` — the exact bug the repo already fixed in `neighbor_table.rs`
- **Severity:** Medium  *(as filed: Critical — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. Becomes High the moment ROUT-4's wiring lands. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (subsumed by SYS-1)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `4b03ae8`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/dedup_cache.rs:62-64` (fn `evict_old`)
- **What:** `evict_old` builds a cutoff by subtracting a 1-hour `Duration` from `Instant::now()`. `impl Sub<Duration> for Instant` is `checked_sub(...).expect("overflow when subtracting duration from instant")`. On Linux/Android `Instant` is `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`, whose epoch is **system boot**, so `Instant::now()` is smaller than 3600 s for the first hour after boot and the subtraction panics. `evict_old` is called unconditionally from `record()` (line 59), i.e. on **every** message the node forwards.
- **Evidence:**
```
59	        self.evict_old();
60	    }
61	
62	    fn evict_old(&mut self) {
63	        let cutoff = Instant::now() - EXACT_WINDOW;
64	        while let Some(front) = self.ring.front() {
```
  and `dedup_cache.rs:19` — `const EXACT_WINDOW: Duration = Duration::from_secs(3600);`
- **Why it is wrong:** The codebase has an in-tree post-mortem of this exact defect, `crates/iris-core/src/discovery/neighbor_table.rs:236-243`: *"`Instant::now() - ttl` overflows and PANICS when process uptime is below the TTL — which is the normal case for an app that autostarts at device boot… the task died silently and neighbour discovery stayed dead for the whole process lifetime."* The fix applied there (`now.duration_since(n.last_seen) >= self.ttl`) was never propagated to the routing module.
- **Root cause:** Copy of the pre-fix `Instant::now() - window` idiom; the neighbor-table fix was applied locally instead of crate-wide.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Android device reboots; IRIS autostarts at T+20 s; the first mesh message is forwarded at T+25 s → `record()` → `evict_old()` → panic `overflow when subtracting duration from instant`. If this runs on a spawned task the task dies silently and routing dedup is dead for the process lifetime; on the main path the node crashes. Reachable from `sim/mod.rs:377` (`self.nodes[dst].forwarded.record(id)`) and `tests/protocol_conformance.rs:356`, so CI on a freshly-booted Linux runner is also affected.
- **Impact:** Panic / silent task death on every node in the first hour after boot — precisely the disaster-response cold-start window this product exists for.
- **Fix:**
```rust
fn evict_old(&mut self) {
    let now = Instant::now();
    while let Some(front) = self.ring.front() {
        if now.duration_since(front.1) > EXACT_WINDOW {
            let (id, _) = self.ring.pop_front().unwrap();
            self.exact.remove(&id);
        } else { break; }
    }
}
```
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `sim/mod.rs:377`, `tests/protocol_conformance.rs:344-361`. Same idiom in ROUT-2 and ROUT-3 must be fixed in the same pass; consider a clippy deny for `Instant - Duration` crate-wide.

#### ROUT-2: `RoutingEngine::prune` panics on `Instant::now() - 3600s`
- **Severity:** Low  *(as filed: High — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. Dead code; blocking-High as a precondition of ROUT-11's wiring. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (subsumed by SYS-1)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `4b03ae8`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/mod.rs:301-302` (fn `prune`)
- **What:** Same `Instant` underflow as ROUT-1, with a 1-hour contact-log retention window.
- **Evidence:**
```
300	        self.routing_table.prune_expired(self.table_ttl);
301	        let cutoff = Instant::now() - Duration::from_secs(3600);
302	        self.contact_log.retain(|_, t| *t >= cutoff);
```
- **Why it is wrong:** Same invariant as ROUT-1 (`neighbor_table.rs:236-243`).
- **Root cause:** Same idiom, same missed propagation.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Any node calling `prune()` within the first hour of boot panics. (Currently masked only because `prune()` is never called anywhere — see ROUT-11 — so wiring the pruner *introduces* the crash.)
- **Impact:** Panic in the maintenance path; wiring ROUT-11 without fixing this converts a leak into a crash.
- **Fix:** `let now = Instant::now(); self.contact_log.retain(|_, t| now.duration_since(*t) < Duration::from_secs(3600));`
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** Must land together with ROUT-11 (wiring `prune`) and ROUT-3.

#### ROUT-3: `RoutingTable::prune_expired` panics on `Instant::now() - expiry`
- **Severity:** Low  *(as filed: High — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (subsumed by SYS-1)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `4b03ae8`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/known_path.rs:77-80` (fn `prune_expired`)
- **What:** Same `Instant` underflow; `expiry` is 600 s by default (`mod.rs:110`, `mod.rs:111`), so the panic window is the first 10 minutes after boot.
- **Evidence:**
```

78	        let cutoff = Instant::now() - expiry;
79	        self.entries.retain(|_, e| e.last_confirmed >= cutoff);
80	    }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** Same invariant as ROUT-1.
- **Root cause:** Same idiom.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Node boots, discovers peers, `prune()` fires at T+120 s → panic. The unit test `prune_expired_entries` (`known_path.rs:171-178`) passes `Duration::from_millis(10)`, which is small enough never to underflow — so the test cannot catch it.

#### ROUT-4: The routing dedup cache is never written — Algorithm 3's anti-loop guarantee does not exist
- **Severity:** Medium  *(as filed: Critical — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. (unwired subsystem whose verification docs claim a guarantee it does not implement); Critical once `RoutingEngine` is put on the forwarding path. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (ROUT-4)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `ade3acd`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/mod.rs:99, 112, 162-164, 253-261` (struct `RoutingEngine`, fn `decide_inner`)
- **What:** `RoutingEngine` owns a `ForwardedCache` but exposes only an immutable accessor (`forward_cache(&self)`) and never calls `record`, `record_peer` or `is_duplicate` on it. `decide_inner` passes `&self.forward_cache` into `recipients_for_flood`, which only ever calls `cache.contains_peer(...)` — a set that nothing ever inserts into. Repo-wide grep: `ForwardedCache::record` is called only from `sim/mod.rs:377`, `dedup_cache.rs` tests, and `tests/protocol_conformance.rs:356`. `is_duplicate` is called only from `sim/mod.rs:315` and tests. **Zero production call sites via `RoutingEngine`.**
- **Evidence:**
```
99	    forward_cache: ForwardedCache,
...
162	    pub fn forward_cache(&self) -> &ForwardedCache {
163	        &self.forward_cache
164	    }
...
257	                hop_count,
258	                &self.forward_cache,
259	                &recipient,
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `mod.rs:12-14` claims *"no duplicate delivery (dedup cache)"* as a correctness guarantee; `BASELINE_ROUTING.md` §Anti-Loop specifies a recently-forwarded set consulted on arrival (*"When a duplicate arrives: silently drop. Do not forward, do not store."*); `CONGESTION_CONTROL.md:247-250` names dedup as **the** anti-flooding mechanism; `ROUTE_VERIFICATION.md:56` asserts *"No-backtrack + dedup-window satisfy the DTN no-loop correctness guarantees."* None of that is true of the shipped `RoutingEngine`.
- **Root cause:** The cache was written and unit-tested in isolation; the call site that would `record()` after a forward (and `is_duplicate()` on arrival) was never added to `decide`/`decide_inner`.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** 4-node ring A–B–C–D–A. P1 message (`max_hops = 5`) originates at A. B floods to C and D; C floods to D and A; D floods to A and C… Each node re-processes every copy because `is_duplicate` is never consulted, and `already_flooded` is a caller-supplied `Vec` the engine never appends to. Copies grow as `(deg−1)^hop` until the hop cap. For P0 the cap is 255 (ROUT-18) → effectively unbounded.
- **Impact:** Flood storm / broadcast amplification, battery and airtime exhaustion, duplicate delivery to the application. A single injected P0 envelope is a network-wide DoS.
- **Fix:** Add `is_duplicate` as the first gate of `decide_inner` (returning `ForwardingDecision::Drop`), and `record(message_id)` + `record_peer` for each chosen recipient after a Flood/Forward decision. This requires threading `MessageId` through `decide` (it currently takes only sender/recipient/hop/priority).
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `RoutingEngine::decide` signature change → `tests/obs_telemetry.rs:91,221`, all `routing/mod.rs` tests, `sim/mod.rs` (which today implements its own parallel dedup), `ROUTE_VERIFICATION.md` criterion 2 must be re-verified.

#### ROUT-5: `routing::store::is_expired` makes far-future-timestamped messages immortal — a re-introduction of a bug the crate already fixed and documented
- **Severity:** Medium  *(as filed: Critical — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. Real, latent; Critical the moment SCF sits behind a transport without the `message_engine` ingestion check in front of it. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (ROUT-5)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `1821c48`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/store.rs:31-34` (fn `is_expired`)
- **What:** `lifetime_start = timestamp.min(now_unix)`. For a forged/skewed timestamp far in the future, `min` always selects `now_unix`, so `now_unix - lifetime_start == 0` on **every** call, forever. The message never expires at any node, at any time.
- **Evidence:**
```
31	pub fn is_expired(now_unix: u64, timestamp: u64, ttl_seconds: u64) -> bool {
32	    let lifetime_start = timestamp.min(now_unix);
33	    now_unix.saturating_sub(lifetime_start) > ttl_seconds
34	}
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `crates/iris-core/src/message_engine/expiry.rs:55-64` documents this precise defect as already-fixed there: *"The previous behaviour returned `false` for them, intending an 'arrival-time lifetime' of `now + ttl`. But no arrival time was ever recorded, so the comparison was re-evaluated against a moving `now` on every call and could never become true: a single envelope with `timestamp = now + 10^9` was immortal at every checkpoint… That is a trivial, permanent memory-exhaustion vector, so this now fails closed."* `expiry.rs:190-197` is the regression test. `REQ-ROUTE-ROUT-022` (ROUTING_REQUIREMENTS.md:68) requires expired bundles MUST be deleted.
- **Root cause:** Two independent `is_expired` implementations in one crate; the `message_engine` one was hardened, the `routing::store` one (which SCF actually uses) was not.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Attacker emits one envelope with `timestamp = u64::MAX`, `ttl_seconds = 1`. Every node that receives it calls `scf.rs:207` → `is_expired(now, u64::MAX, 1)` → `min(u64::MAX, now) = now` → `0 > 1` = false → buffered. `scf.rs:307` (`expire_stale`) filters with the same predicate → never removed. `scf.rs:267` keeps ranking it as live forever.
- **Impact:** Permanent store-carry-forward buffer occupancy on every node in the mesh, from a single unsigned field. Combined with P0 priority (never evicted, per `INV-ROUTE-003`) this is a permanent memory-exhaustion DoS.
- **Fix:** Delete `routing::store::is_expired` and re-export `message_engine::expiry::is_expired` (fails closed on skew-suspect), or `is_expired_from_arrival` where SCF records an arrival instant (it does — `ScfMessage` has a stored-at time).
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `scf.rs:22, 207, 267, 307` (out of scope but must be re-verified), `store.rs:70-76` test (which currently asserts the buggy behaviour — see ROUT-31), `SCF_VERIFICATION.md`, `STORE_SECURITY_REVIEW.md`.

---

#### ROUT-6: Algorithm 4 never checks TTL; `store_or_drop` / `ShouldStore` / `StoreAction` are dead, and `ForwardingDecision::Drop` is unconstructable
- **Severity:** Medium  *(as filed: High — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (ROUT-6)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `50d3a9b`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/mod.rs:268-269` (fn `decide_inner`); `crates/iris-core/src/routing/store.rs:20-26, 38-49`
- **What:** `decide_inner`'s terminal branch is a bare `ForwardingDecision::Store` with no TTL evaluation. `decide` does not take a timestamp, ttl, or message id, so it *cannot* evaluate TTL. `store_or_drop`, `ShouldStore`, `StoreAction` and `build_store_action` have no callers outside `store.rs`'s own tests and the `mod.rs:47` re-export (repo-wide grep). `ForwardingDecision::Drop` is constructed **nowhere** in the crate — the only occurrence outside the enum definition is the label arm at `mod.rs:90`.
- **Evidence:**
```
265	        } else if hop_count >= policy.max_hops {
266	            // Hop budget exhausted — fall through to Store.
267	        }
268	        // Algorithm 4: Store.
269	        ForwardingDecision::Store
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `mod.rs:13-15` promises *"no zombie messages (TTL checked at every decision)"*. `BASELINE_ROUTING.md` Algorithm 4 opens with *"Check TTL — don't store expired messages"* returning `Dropped { reason: TtlExpired }`. `ROUTE_VERIFICATION.md:27` claims store.rs implements *"Algorithm 4: TTL re-check"*. The engine never performs it.
- **Root cause:** `decide()`'s signature was designed around `(sender, recipient, hop, priority)` and never extended with the envelope's expiry fields; `store.rs` was written to the spec but left unwired.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** An envelope with `ttl_seconds = 60` and `timestamp = now − 10_000` reaches a node with no neighbors. `decide` returns `Store`. The caller stores an already-dead message; it is re-evaluated at every future contact and forwarded on.
- **Impact:** Zombie messages consume storage and airtime past their TTL; `REQ-ROUTE-ROUT-022` (expiry MUST be enforced + expiry event emitted) is unmet; the `Drop` telemetry label can never appear, so the observability dashboard's drop counter is permanently zero.
- **Fix:** Extend `decide` with `now_unix, timestamp, ttl_seconds` (or an `&Envelope`), gate the whole chain on `store::is_expired` (fixed per ROUT-5) returning `ForwardingDecision::Drop`, and use `store_or_drop` for the terminal branch.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `decide` signature → `tests/obs_telemetry.rs`, `routing/mod.rs` tests, `ROUTE_VERIFICATION.md` criteria 1 and 5.

#### ROUT-7: GTMX+ `max_dp_seen` is keyed per `(candidate, destination)`, not per message — the opportunistic layer works exactly once per neighbor/destination pair, forever
- **Severity:** Medium  *(as filed: High — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (ROUT-7)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `eac839f`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/opportunistic.rs:103-104, 164-170, 196-205` (fields `max_dp_seen`, fns `gtmx_advantage`, `decide`)
- **What:** The anti-oscillation guard is documented (and specified) as per-message state, but neither `gtmx_advantage` nor `decide` receives a message id. The key is `(candidate_peer, destination)`. Once `decide` picks neighbor `B` for destination `D` with DP `p`, `max_dp_seen[(B,D)] = p`; every **subsequent, unrelated** message to `D` finds `p <= seen + eps` and rejects `B`.
- **Evidence:**
```
103	    /// (sender, recipient) → highest DP this node has seen for that message.
104	    max_dp_seen: HashMap<(PeerId, PeerId), f64>,
...
166	        let key = (*candidate, *dest);
167	        let seen = self.max_dp_seen.get(&key).copied().unwrap_or(0.0);
168	        if p_candidate <= seen + DP_FLOOR_EPS {
169	            return false;
170	        }
...
198	                let key = (nb, *dest);
199	                let e = self.max_dp_seen.entry(key).or_insert(0.0);
200	                *e = p.max(*e);
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `ROUTE2_DESIGN.md:52-53` — *"**P_max monotonicity (GTMX+ anti-oscillation guard)**: track **per-message** `max_dp_seen`; never forward to a node with DP ≤ previously seen maximum."* `ROUTE2_VERIFICATION.md:26-27` repeats *"per-message `max_dp_seen` monotonicity guard"*. The code has no per-message dimension at all. The doc comment on line 103 even says "for that message" while the type says otherwise.
- **Root cause:** `decide()` was given the signature `(dest, candidates, priority, hop_budget)` with no message id; the per-message key was silently collapsed to the candidate id.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Ferry node `F` has a stable `P(F,D) = 0.82`. Node `A` (`P(A,D)=0.2`) meets `F` and forwards message M1 → `max_dp_seen[(F,D)] = 0.82`. Ten minutes later `A` has M2, M3 … Mn for `D` and meets `F` again with the same DP → `0.82 <= 0.82 + 1e-6` → `NoAdvantage` → all subsequent messages fall through to Flood/Store. The best relay in the network is permanently blacklisted for that destination.
- **Impact:** ROUTE-002 delivers at most one message per (relay, destination) pair for the whole process lifetime; every later message reverts to L0 flooding — the delivery-rate and overhead-ratio improvements ROUTE2_VERIFICATION claims are not realised in steady state.
- **Fix:** Key on `(MessageId, PeerId /*dest*/)` and add a `message_id: &MessageId` parameter to `gtmx_advantage`/`decide`; evict entries when the message is delivered or expires (see ROUT-14).
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `benches/routing.rs:51-60` (which currently measures the degenerate path — ROUT-32), `sim/mod.rs` opportunistic path, `opportunistic.rs:278-327` tests (none of which call `decide` twice), `ROUTE2_VERIFICATION.md` criteria 3 and 4.

#### ROUT-8: A `NaN` delivery predictability passes every GTMX+ guard and wins over all honest candidates
- **Severity:** Medium  *(as filed: High — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** PARTIALLY-CORRECT. (missing input validation on a public API that will be fed wire data later), not High. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (ROUT-8)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `6f8eda8`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/opportunistic.rs:146-173, 187-194` (fns `gtmx_advantage`, `decide`)
- **What:** All three rejection tests are `<=` comparisons against `p_candidate`. Every IEEE-754 comparison with `NaN` is false, so a `NaN` candidate falls through all three `return false` guards and `gtmx_advantage` returns `true`. In `decide`, the tie-break `*p > *bp` is also false for `NaN`, so once a `NaN` candidate becomes `best` no honest candidate can displace it. Finally `*e = p.max(*e)` — `f64::max` returns the **non-NaN** operand — so `max_dp_seen` is written as `0.0` and the attacker wins again on the next call.
- **Evidence:**
```
154	        if p_candidate <= self.pred.config().p_first_threshold {
155	            return false;
156	        }
157	        let p_self = self.p_for(dest);
158	        if p_candidate <= p_self + DP_FLOOR_EPS {
159	            return false;
160	        }
...
168	        if p_candidate <= seen + DP_FLOOR_EPS {
169	            return false;
170	        }
...
190	                && best.as_ref().map(|(_, bp)| *p > *bp).unwrap_or(true)
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `ROUTE2_DESIGN.md:128` lists *"Rogue node inflates its DP"* with the mitigation *"GTMX+ P_max monotonicity"*. `NaN` defeats the monotonicity guard entirely — it is strictly stronger than "inflate to 1.0" (which would at least be recorded in `max_dp_seen` and self-limit on the next round). Note that the sibling `prophet.rs:230` *does* defend (`p_other_dst.clamp(0.0,1.0)` then `if p_t > p_old_t` rejects NaN); `opportunistic.rs` does not, and its `candidates` slice is caller-supplied from the peer's `CapabilityBundle` snapshot.
- **Root cause:** Guards written as "reject if not better" (`<=`) rather than "accept only if better" (`>`), which is not NaN-safe; no input validation at the L2 boundary.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Attacker `X` advertises `P(X,D) = f64::NAN` (an all-ones f64 bit pattern, or a `0.0/0.0` result of decoding a malformed f32). `A` runs `decide(&D, &[(X, NaN), (F, 0.9)], P1, 5)` → `ForwardTo { next_hop: X }`. `max_dp_seen[(X,D)] = NaN.max(0.0) = 0.0`, so the attack repeats indefinitely while the honest ferry `F` at 0.9 is never selected.
- **Impact:** Deterministic single-copy blackhole: an attacker attracts 100 % of the opportunistic traffic for every destination, permanently. This is the routing-layer sinkhole attack `ROUTING_SECURITY.md` claims is mitigated.
- **Fix:** Sanitise at entry — `if !p_candidate.is_finite() { return false; }` as the first line of `gtmx_advantage`; use `total_cmp` for the best-candidate tie-break; clamp incoming DPs to `[0,1]` before they reach `decide`.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `sim/mod.rs` opportunistic path; add a NaN/∞ unit test alongside `opportunistic.rs:262-327`; `ROUTE2_VERIFICATION.md` threat table.

#### ROUT-9: `contains_peer` is a permanent, message-independent flood blacklist backed by an unbounded, never-pruned set
- **Severity:** Low  *(as filed: High — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. Today (dead field on a dead path). Worth keeping as a **design trap** annotation on the ROUT-4 fix: the obvious wiring is wrong and would break flooding. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (ROUT-9)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `367b2dc`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/flood.rs:60`; `crates/iris-core/src/routing/dedup_cache.rs:30, 75-83`
- **What:** `recipients_for_flood` excludes any neighbor present in `ForwardedCache::peers_seen`. `peers_seen` is a `HashSet<[u8;32]>` with (a) **no message dimension** — an entry excludes the peer from *every* future flood of *every* message; (b) **no expiry** — `evict_old` (line 62) only touches `ring`/`exact`, never `peers_seen`; (c) **no capacity bound**.
- **Evidence:**
```
flood.rs:57	        if nb.peer_id == sender
flood.rs:58	            || nb.peer_id == *recipient
flood.rs:59	            || already_flooded.contains(&nb.peer_id)
flood.rs:60	            || cache.contains_peer(nb.peer_id.as_bytes())
```
```
dedup_cache.rs:75	    pub fn record_peer(&mut self, peer: [u8; 32]) {
dedup_cache.rs:76	        self.peers_seen.insert(peer);
dedup_cache.rs:77	    }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `BASELINE_ROUTING.md` §Algorithm 3 scopes the already-flooded set to a single message (`already_flooded_to: &mut HashSet<NodeId>`, reset per message). A cross-message,永-lived exclusion set is not in any spec and directly contradicts the *"Eventual delivery"* correctness guarantee: a peer excluded once can never receive any flooded message again.
- **Root cause:** `peers_seen` was bolted onto the message-id cache as a "flood hint" (line 74 comment) without the per-message and expiry semantics the message-id side has.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Once ROUT-4 is fixed by calling `record_peer` after a flood (the obvious wiring, given the field exists), node A floods message M1 to neighbors {B,C,D} and records all three. M2 arrives → `recipients_for_flood` returns `[]` → `decide_inner` falls to `Store`. A never floods again for the rest of the process. Separately, on the current code path the set is pure attack surface: a caller that records observed peers grows the set with every distinct 32-byte peer id an attacker mints (32 B + hash overhead each, unbounded).
- **Impact:** Total loss of flood forwarding after the first message (once wired), plus unbounded RAM growth driven by attacker-chosen peer ids.
- **Fix:** Either delete `peers_seen`/`record_peer`/`contains_peer` and rely on the per-message `already_flooded` set, or re-key to `HashSet<(MessageId, [u8;32])>` with the same ring-buffer expiry and a hard capacity bound.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `flood.rs:60`, `dedup_cache.rs:129-137` test, `ROUTE_VERIFICATION.md:26` ("peer-dedup hints").

#### ROUT-10: The Bloom filter contributes nothing — `bloom AND exact` collapses to `exact`, cutting the dedup window from 24 h/72 h to 1 h
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (ROUT-10)  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `a95ed8d`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/dedup_cache.rs:46-51` (fn `is_duplicate`)
- **What:** A Bloom filter has no false negatives, so `bloom.contains(x)` is `true` for every `x` ever inserted. `is_duplicate` therefore evaluates to `bloom.contains(x) && exact.contains(x)` ≡ `exact.contains(x)`. Since `evict_old` removes from `exact` after 1 h but **never** clears the bloom, the ~351 KB bitmap and its ~10 hash probes per lookup are pure overhead, and the effective dedup window is `EXACT_WINDOW` = 1 hour.
- **Evidence:**
```
46	    pub fn is_duplicate(&self, id: &MessageId) -> bool {
47	        if !self.bloom.contains(id.to_bytes()) {
48	            return false;
49	        }
50	        self.exact.contains(id)
51	    }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** The module header (`dedup_cache.rs:3`) says *"Rolling 24-hour window"*; `BASELINE_ROUTING.md` §Anti-Loop says *"a rolling window of message IDs it has forwarded in the last 24 hours"*; `ROUTING_SECURITY.md:72` relies on *"the deduplication Bloom filter … within the active 72-hour window"* as the replay-attack mitigation. The delivered window is 1 hour. (The spec's own `DeduplicationCache` sketch has the same `&&` flaw, so the code faithfully reproduces a design error — but the stated 24 h/72 h property is what the security analysis depends on.)
- **Root cause:** Faithful transcription of the pseudo-code in `BASELINE_ROUTING.md:163-168` without noticing that the exact set, not the bloom, becomes the limiting term once the bloom is never aged.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Attacker captures a P0 evacuation-order bundle at T, replays it at T+90 min. `exact` no longer holds the id → `is_duplicate` false → re-forwarded and re-delivered mesh-wide. `ROUTING_SECURITY.md:232` rates replay prevention "Strong".
- **Impact:** Replay window 24×–72× shorter than the security model assumes; 351 KB of dead RAM per `ForwardedCache` (see ROUT-26).
- **Fix:** Make the bloom the long window and the exact set the false-positive confirmer: `if !bloom.contains(x) { return false } ; if exact.contains(x) { return true } ; /* bloom hit, outside exact window */ true` — accepting the 0.1 % FPR as the design intends — and rotate the bloom (two-generation rolling filter) at the 24 h boundary so it does not saturate.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `sim/mod.rs:315`, `tests/protocol_conformance.rs:344-361`, `BASELINE_ROUTING.md` pseudo-code should be corrected too.

#### ROUT-11: `RoutingEngine::prune()` is never called — routing table and contact log grow without bound
- **Severity:** Low  *(as filed: High — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. (missing wiring in an unwired subsystem). Must still be listed as a prerequisite item for whoever wires the engine, together with ROUT-2/ROUT-3. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `440f610`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/mod.rs:298-311` (fn `prune`)
- **What:** Repo-wide grep for `.prune()` finds no caller of `RoutingEngine::prune` anywhere in `crates/` (only `prophet::prune` and unrelated names). `routing_table` (`HashMap<PeerId, RouteEntry>`, `known_path.rs:29`) and `contact_log` (`HashMap<PeerId, Instant>`, `mod.rs:100`) are therefore append-only for the process lifetime. There is no background task, no timer, no call from `decide` or `record_contact`.
- **Evidence:**
```
298	    pub fn prune(&mut self) {
299	        let before = self.routing_table.len();
300	        self.routing_table.prune_expired(self.table_ttl);
```
  `record_contact` (line 169-179) inserts into both maps and never prunes.
- **Why it is wrong:** `BASELINE_ROUTING.md` §Algorithm 2 — *"entries expire after 10 minutes of no confirmation"*. `ROUTE_VERIFICATION.md:39` claims criterion 3 (*"RoutingTable entries expire after 10 min"*) ✅ PASS on the strength of a unit test that calls `prune_expired` directly. In the assembled engine, entries never expire.
- **Root cause:** Maintenance entry point written but never scheduled; the verification doc tested the leaf function rather than the wiring.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A phone in a dense crowd sees 5,000 distinct peers over a day. `record_contact` inserts 5,000 `RouteEntry` (2 × 32 B PeerId + `String` transport + `Instant` ≈ 100 B) and 5,000 `contact_log` entries, none ever removed. `try_known_path` then keeps returning stale next hops for peers that left hours ago, each costing a neighbor-table lock round-trip before being invalidated.
- **Impact:** Unbounded RAM growth proportional to lifetime peer count; stale routes cause repeated failed forwarding attempts. `ROUTING_SECURITY.md:76` ("exhausting routing table memory on legitimate nodes") is unmitigated at L0.
- **Fix:** Call `prune()` from a periodic maintenance task, or opportunistically from `decide` (rate-limited to once per N seconds). Fix ROUT-2 and ROUT-3 first or the wiring introduces a boot-time panic.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** Whoever owns the routing task loop; ROUT-2, ROUT-3, ROUT-13.

#### ROUT-12: `RoutingTable::upsert` unconditionally overwrites — any peer can replace a good route with a worse or bogus one
- **Severity:** Medium  *(as filed: High — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED-BUT-DOWNGRADED. (dead fields + missing route-preference comparison, no attacker path today), not High. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `440f610`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/known_path.rs:43-62` (fn `upsert`); `crates/iris-core/src/routing/mod.rs:171-172`
- **What:** `upsert` is a bare `HashMap::insert`. It never compares the incoming `hop_count` or `quality` against the existing entry. Last writer wins, regardless of route quality, hop count, or the trustworthiness of the advertiser. `best_route` (line 38-40) is therefore a misnomer: there is exactly one candidate and no selection.
- **Evidence:**
```
51	        self.entries.insert(
52	            destination,
53	            RouteEntry {
54	                destination,
55	                next_hop,
56	                transport,
57	                hop_count,
58	                quality,
59	                last_confirmed: Instant::now(),
60	            },
61	        );
```
  `RouteEntry.hop_count` and `.quality` are written here and read **nowhere** — `try_known_path` (lines 92-107) uses only `next_hop`.
- **Why it is wrong:** `BASELINE_ROUTING.md` §Algorithm 2 specifies `routing_table.best_route(&msg.recipient, msg.priority)` — a priority-aware *selection*, and the entry carries `delivery_probability` and `hop_count` precisely so a better route can win. `ROUTING_SECURITY.md` §2.5 assumes routing advertisements are bounded and vetted.
- **Root cause:** A single-entry map was chosen as an MVP; the quality/hop fields were kept from the spec's `RouteEntry` but never used in a comparison.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** `record_contact(D, "ble")` at `mod.rs:171-172` installs `D → D, hop_count 1, Good`. A neighbor then advertises "I can reach D in 9 hops over a poor link"; the handler calls `upsert(D, X, "lora", 9, Poor)`. The 1-hop route is destroyed. More seriously, an attacker advertises a route to *every* destination it observes and unconditionally becomes the next hop for all of them — a routing-table sinkhole that requires no DP manipulation at all.
- **Impact:** Route quality regression, and an unauthenticated route-poisoning / blackhole primitive at L0.
- **Fix:** Compare before replacing: accept only if `next_hop == existing.next_hop` (a refresh), or `hop_count < existing.hop_count`, or `hop_count == existing.hop_count && quality > existing.quality`, or the existing entry is past `expiry`. Then actually consume `hop_count`/`quality` in `try_known_path`.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `mod.rs:171` (`record_contact` must be exempt or always win with hop_count 1), `known_path.rs:130-146` tests, `MULTIPATH_ROUTING.md` if multiple entries per destination are eventually needed.

#### ROUT-13: `RoutingTable` has no capacity bound
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed  ·  Tier 2  ·  commit `440f610`  ·  2026-08-26
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/routing/known_path.rs:27-30, 43-62`
- **What:** `entries: HashMap<PeerId, RouteEntry>` with no maximum, no LRU, no eviction other than the (never-invoked, see ROUT-11) time-based prune. Every distinct destination an attacker advertises adds a permanent entry.
- **Evidence:**
```
27	#[derive(Debug, Default)]
28	pub struct RoutingTable {
29	    entries: HashMap<PeerId, RouteEntry>,
30	}
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `ROUTING_SECURITY.md:76-78` names this exact attack (*"Attacker floods the network with large numbers of fake bundle IDs or false PRoPHET updates, exhausting routing table memory"*) and claims the mitigation *"PRoPHET table is bounded (1,000 entries max)"*. The PRoPHET table **is** bounded (`prophet.rs:27`, `MAX_DP_ENTRIES = 4096`); the L0 routing table is not bounded at all. `BASELINE_ROUTING.md` §Resource Budget sizes it at 10,000 entries / ~2 MB.

- **Fix:** Add `MAX_ROUTE_ENTRIES` (10_000 per the spec) with lowest-quality/highest-hop-count eviction on insert, mirroring `prophet.rs:190-200`.
