#### BLE-10: A partially-written message leaves the peer's reassembler permanently poisoned; no in-flight tracking
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:829-842` (fn `send`)
- **What:** `send` writes frames in a loop and aborts on the first failure. Frames already delivered
  stay in the peer's reassembler with no abort signal, and the sender keeps no record of what was
  in flight.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
829          for frame in &frames {
830              if let Err(e) = adapter.gatt_write(handle, char_uuid, frame.clone()) {
834                  self.close_peer(peer, adapter.clone(), Some(&e));
835                  return Err(to_transport_err(e));
836              }
837          }
838          Ok(SendReceipt { peer_id: *peer, bytes_sent: message.payload.len(), ... })
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `bytes_sent: message.payload.len()` on the success path counts the *unsegmented*
  payload, ignoring the 6-byte-per-frame header, so the receipt is wrong for every multi-chunk message
  (a 30 KB message at MTU 23 is ~2500 frames = ~15 KB of header the receipt never mentions). And on
  the failure path there is nothing that tells the peer to discard the partial.
- **Root cause:** `send` is fire-and-forget: there is no per-message state on the sender, no ACK, and
  no cancel frame in the wire format (ble_att.rs:9-14 defines total/msg_id/idx/count and nothing else).
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A 30 KB P0 message at MTU 23 → ~2500 `gatt_write` calls. Write 1800
  fails. The peer holds 1799 chunks of msg_id N for the full 30 s `REASSEMBLY_TTL`, occupying one of
  its 64 partial slots and up to ~130 KB. The engine retries the same message and — because
  `alloc_msg_id` is a shared monotonic counter — gets a *different* msg_id, so the poisoned slot is
  never reused, just orphaned.
- **Impact:** Under a lossy link, a sender can exhaust its own peer's 64 partial slots with orphaned
  retries and lock itself out for 30 s at a time. `bytes_sent` under-reports by the header overhead,
  corrupting any byte accounting or cost model built on `SendReceipt`.
- **Fix:** (a) `bytes_sent: frames.iter().map(Vec::len).sum()`. (b) Add an abort frame (e.g. `count = 0`
  with the msg_id) and send it on the failure path so the receiver can free the slot immediately.
  (c) Track in-flight `msg_id`s per peer so `close_peer` can report which messages were lost.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `Reassembler::push` needs an abort arm; `SendReceipt` consumers;
  re-verify `large_message_segments_across_mtu_and_reassembles`, `rt005_write_failure_tears_down_dead_peer`.

#### BLE-11: `parse_mac` silently converts malformed input into a valid-looking address
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:897-904` (fn `parse_mac`), called at `:702`
- **What:** Non-hex octets become `0`, fewer than six octets leave the remainder as `0`, and there is
  no error return at all.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
898  fn parse_mac(s: &str) -> BleAddress {
899      let mut b = [0u8; 6];
900      for (i, part) in s.split(':').take(6).enumerate() {
901          b[i] = u8::from_str_radix(part, 16).unwrap_or(0);
902      }
903      BleAddress(b)
904  }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `""` → `00:00:00:00:00:00`. `"garbage"` → `00:00:00:00:00:00`. `"AA:BB"` →
  `AA:BB:00:00:00:00`. All are then handed to `connect_gatt` as if they were addresses. The
  `transport_addresses` vector is caller-supplied (`PeerInfo`, message.rs) and may originate from
  persisted peer state or a remote hint, so it is not trusted input.
- **Root cause:** The function is infallible by signature; `connect` at :698-703 already has a
  `PeerNotFound` error path it could have used.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Two `PeerInfo` records with different malformed BLE addresses both
  map to `BleAddress([0;6])`. `connect()` dials the same nonsense address twice, and on the Android
  bridge `hex_to_ble_addr(..).unwrap_or(BleAddress([0u8;6]))` (bridge.rs:203) does the identical
  collapse in the inbound direction, so two distinct scanned devices can merge into one entry.
- **Impact:** Wasted 30 s GATT dials against `00:00:00:00:00:00`, plus a peer-identity aliasing
  primitive if malformed addresses can be injected.
- **Fix:** `fn parse_mac(s: &str) -> Option<BleAddress>` — require exactly 6 parts, propagate the
  radix error, and map `None` to `TransportError::PeerNotFound` at the call site. Do the same in both
  bridges' `hex_to_ble_addr`/`hex_to_uuid` (drop the result instead of substituting zeros).
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `connect` (:698-703); both bridges' `scan_results`/
  `incoming_gatt_writes`. Re-verify `mac_parser_works` (which only covers the happy path — see BLE-24).

#### BLE-12: `to_transport_err` collapses three distinct, differently-actionable failures into `NotSupported`
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:888-895` (fn `to_transport_err`)
- **What:** `PermissionDenied`, `AdapterOff` and `NotSupported` all map to `TransportError::NotSupported`.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
888  fn to_transport_err(e: BleError) -> TransportError {
889      match e {
890          BleError::NotSupported => TransportError::NotSupported,
891          BleError::PermissionDenied | BleError::AdapterOff => TransportError::NotSupported,
892          BleError::DeviceNotFound => TransportError::PeerNotFound,
893          BleError::GattFailure(m) => TransportError::Protocol(m),
894      }
895  }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** These demand three different user actions — grant a runtime permission, turn
  the radio on, and (nothing, the hardware is absent). `TransportError` has no variant that carries the
  distinction and no free-form field is used here, so the information is destroyed at the boundary; a
  UI layer receiving `NotSupported` cannot render a "Turn on Bluetooth" affordance.
- **Root cause:** `TransportError` (error.rs:7-27) has no permission/hardware-state variants; the
  mapping took the nearest available one instead of using `Protocol(String)` or extending the enum.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** First run on Android 12+: the user has not yet granted
  `BLUETOOTH_SCAN`. `discover_peers` → `start_scan` → `PermissionDenied` → `NotSupported`. The app
  concludes the device has no BLE and stops offering it — permanently, with no prompt.
- **Impact:** Users on a permission-gated OS silently lose the BLE transport with no recovery path.
  Directly undermines the emergency-mesh use case.
- **Fix:** Add `TransportError::PermissionDenied` and `TransportError::HardwareOff` to error.rs and map
  them through; at minimum use `Protocol(format!("ble: {e}"))` so the string survives.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `error.rs`, every `TransportError` match in the engine/FFI,
  `no_adapter_returns_not_supported`, `rt004_connect_failure_restores_available`
  (which asserts `assert_ne!(err, NotSupported)` and would need updating).

#### BLE-13: `.drain(..).take(n)` silently destroys every scan result past `max_peers`
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:560-564` (fn `discover_peers`)
- **What:** `Vec::drain(..)` removes the entire range when the `Drain` guard is dropped, regardless of
  how many items `take(n)` consumed. Results beyond `max_peers` are removed from the adapter queue and
  discarded, not left for the next pass.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
556          // Advert floods are bounded BEFORE materializing the Vec (BLE-RT-C007) — the
557          // cap applies to allocation, not just the candidate output.
560          let results: Vec<ScanResult> = adapter
561              .scan_results()
562              .drain(..)
563              .take(config.max_peers)
564              .collect();
```
- **Why it is wrong:** The comment claims allocation bounding, which is true, but omits that the
  discarded results are *destroyed*. Test `rt013_discovery_enforces_max_peers` (ble.rs:1818-1846)
  injects 5 results with `max_peers: 2` and asserts 2 candidates — it never checks that the other 3
  survive for a later call. They do not.
- **Root cause:** Misreading `Drain`'s drop semantics: `take(n)` bounds consumption, not removal.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A crowded environment (conference, disaster shelter) with 100
  ambient adverts, `max_peers` at the default 64. The 36 results past the cap are destroyed. Because
  BLE advert order is essentially arbitrary and the adapter queue is FIFO, the *same* peers can be cut
  every pass, so a specific IRIS peer may never be discovered.
- **Impact:** Discovery starvation exactly when the mesh is densest. An attacker can weaponise it by
  flooding cheap adverts to push real IRIS beacons past the cap.
- **Fix:** Split the drain explicitly so the tail is preserved:
```rust
let results: Vec<ScanResult> = {
    let mut q = adapter.scan_results();
    let n = q.len().min(config.max_peers);
    q.drain(..n).collect()          // leaves the remainder queued for the next pass
};
```
  and separately bound total queue length in the adapter to stop unbounded growth.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `rt013_discovery_enforces_max_peers`,
  `c001_ios_leg_probe_budget_caps_probe_connects`, `c001_android_leg_never_probe_connects_empty_ads`.

#### BLE-14: Blocking GATT connect/read/disconnect inside a synchronous closure in an async fn, with no timeout
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:583-605` (fn `discover_peers`, connect-to-identify branch)
- **What:** Up to 8 full connect→read→disconnect cycles run synchronously inside `filter_map`, on the
  async executor thread, with no timeout and every error discarded by `.ok()`.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
593                      if *probe_guard == probe_budget { return None; }
594                      *probe_guard += 1;
595                      let handle = adapter.connect_gatt(r.address).ok()?;
596                      let payload = adapter.gatt_read(handle, IRIS_IDENTIFY_CHARACTERISTIC).ok();
599                      adapter.disconnect_gatt(handle);
600                      DiscoveryBeacon::parse(&payload?).ok()
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `iris-ios/src/ffi/ble_adapter.rs:73-77` states that the BLE-RT-C003 timeout is
  "enforced by the Swift side and surfaced as `IrisFfiError::Timeout`" — the Rust side has no timeout
  of its own and, worse, cannot even observe the Swift one because `.ok()` discards it. There is no
  `.await` anywhere in the closure, so the executor thread is held for the whole probe sequence.
- **Root cause:** `filter_map` over a `Vec` was the shortest way to express "probe if empty"; making it
  async would have required `stream::iter(...).then(...)`.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** 8 out-of-range iOS peers. Each `connect_gatt` blocks for the
  CoreBluetooth connect timeout. Even at a generous 5 s each, `discover_peers` blocks one tokio worker
  for 40 s while claiming to be async.
- **Impact:** Executor starvation during discovery; a bad-neighbourhood scan can freeze the runtime.
  All probe failures are invisible — the caller cannot distinguish "no IRIS peers nearby" from "every
  probe timed out".
- **Fix:** Convert to an async pipeline with an explicit per-probe deadline:
```rust
let beacon = tokio::time::timeout(PROBE_TIMEOUT,
    tokio::task::spawn_blocking(move || { /* connect / read / disconnect */ })).await;
```
  and log/count each failure class instead of `.ok()`.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `ios_connect_to_identify_yields_candidate_from_identify_characteristic`,
  `ios_empty_ad_without_identify_yields_no_candidate`, `c001_ios_leg_probe_budget_caps_probe_connects`,
  `android_and_ios_carriers_share_one_beacon_parser` (all synchronous today).

#### BLE-15: Advertising/scan handles are never cleared, and a failed re-advertise leaves a stale handle behind
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:637-679` (`start_advertising`, `stop_advertising`), `:630-635` (`stop_discovery`)
- **What:** `stop_advertising`/`stop_discovery` call the adapter but never set the handle slot back to
  `None`; and if `start_advertising` fails at :669 after already stopping the prior set at :643, the
  slot keeps the *old, now-stopped* handle.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
642          if let Some(prior) = *self.adv_handle.lock().unwrap() {
643              adapter.stop_advertising(prior);          // prior stopped...
...
663          let handle = adapter
664              .start_advertising(AdvertisementData { ... })
669              .map_err(to_transport_err)?;              // ...but on error we return here
670          *self.adv_handle.lock().unwrap() = Some(handle);  // never reached
```
```rust
674      async fn stop_advertising(&self) -> Result<(), TransportError> {
675          if let Some(h) = *self.adv_handle.lock().unwrap() {
676              self.adapter()?.stop_advertising(h);
677          }
678          Ok(())                                         // adv_handle still Some(h)
679      }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** After the failure path, the transport believes it is advertising with handle
  `h` when nothing is advertising. The next `start_advertising` calls `stop_advertising(h)` on a
  handle the OS has already released — undefined behaviour on the Android advertising-set API, and at
  minimum a wasted call. Both stop paths also hold the mutex across the FFI call.
- **Root cause:** The BLE-RT-011 fix (stop-before-restart) was added at the top of the function without
  revisiting the error path or the stop functions.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Identity rotation calls `start_advertising` again. The Android
  advertising-set budget (~4) is already exhausted, so `start_advertising` returns `GattFailure`. The
  node is now advertising nothing, but the transport records a live handle and reports no problem.
- **Impact:** Silent invisibility — the node stops being discoverable and neither the transport state
  nor any log reflects it.
- **Fix:** Clear the slot in three places: set `*adv_handle = None` immediately after the prior stop
  at :643, in `stop_advertising` after the call, and in `stop_discovery` for `scan_handle`. Copy the
  handle out and drop the guard before the FFI call.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `rt011_readvertise_stops_prior_handle`,
  `scan_and_advertising_handles_round_trip` (both assert on stop counts and would need updating).

#### BLE-16: BLE inbound drops are invisible; Wi-Fi Aware counts the same event
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:779-785` vs `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:788-798`
- **What:** The BLE poller discards the send result; the Wi-Fi Aware poller increments a counter for
  the identical failure.
- **Evidence** — BLE:
```rust
779                              let _ = incoming.send(IncomingMessage {
780                                  peer_id,
781                                  transport_id: tid.0.clone(),
782                                  payload,
783                                  received_at: std::time::Instant::now(),
784                              });
```
  Wi-Fi Aware:
```rust
788                      if incoming_tx.send(IncomingMessage { ... }).is_err() {
797                          dropped_inbound.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
798                      }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `broadcast::Sender::send` returns `Err` when there are **zero** subscribers.
  `incoming_messages()` (ble.rs:845-847) subscribes lazily, so every message that arrives before the
  engine calls it is destroyed with no trace. That window is real: `connect()` spawns the poller at
  :744, but nothing forces a subscriber to exist first.
- **Root cause:** The `let _ =` idiom was applied to a `Result` that genuinely carries information.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Engine calls `connect(peer)`, peer immediately writes a message,
  engine then calls `incoming_messages()`. The first message is gone. No log, no counter, no receipt.
- **Impact:** Undiagnosable message loss at connection setup. Note the *lag* case is handled — mod.rs:311-317
  counts `RecvError::Lagged` into `INBOUND_LAGGED_TOTAL` — so this is specifically the no-subscriber
  path that is unaccounted.
- **Fix:** Mirror the Wi-Fi Aware pattern: give `BleTransport` a `dropped_inbound: Arc<AtomicU64>`,
  increment on `Err`, and `tracing::warn!` the first occurrence. Better: subscribe once in `new()` and
  hold the receiver so the channel always has a subscriber.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `gatt_write_flows_into_incoming` and every poller test races this
  window today (they pass because the 50 ms poll gives the test time to subscribe — see BLE-24).

#### BLE-17: Scan backoff escalates permanently and is never reset by a successful scan
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:477-512` (fn `scan_allowed`)
- **What:** `scan_backoff_s` only ever grows. Nothing resets it after a quiet period or a successful
  scan, so the backoff ratchets to the 30 s cap over the app's lifetime. There is also a TOCTOU
  between the `refused_until` read guard (:489) and the write (:507).
- **Evidence:**
```rust
496          if times.len() >= SCAN_CEILING {
498              let mut backoff = self.scan_backoff_s.lock().unwrap();
499              *backoff = if *backoff == 0 { 1 } else { (*backoff * 2).min(SCAN_BACKOFF_MAX_S) };
504              let wait = *backoff;
505              drop(backoff);
506              let until = now + std::time::Duration::from_secs(wait);
507              *self.refused_until.write().unwrap() = Some(until);
508              return false;
509          }
510          times.push_back(now);
```
- **Why it is wrong:** Exponential backoff without a success-reset is not backoff, it is a ratchet.
  After five refusals spread over hours, a burst that would have cost 1 s costs 30 s. Also: the window
  counts only *starts* (`times.push_back` at :510), while the documented Android rule (RES-0019 R6.2,
  quoted at :472-476) is ">= 5 start/stop per 30 s" — `stop_discovery` never touches `scan_times`, so
  half the throttled operations are uncounted.
- **Root cause:** The reset was never written; the start/stop asymmetry follows from `stop_discovery`
  not participating in the throttle bookkeeping.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Two concurrent `discover_peers` calls both find `times.len() >= 5`,
  both double the backoff (1 → 2 → 4 for a single burst), and both write `refused_until`. Over a long
  session the transport reaches the 30 s cap and stays there, so post-outage rediscovery is slow
  exactly when speed matters.
- **Impact:** Degraded and slowly-worsening discovery latency; failure to model the OS throttle it was
  written to respect.
- **Fix:** Reset on success — when `times` is empty at entry (a full quiet window), set
  `*scan_backoff_s.lock().unwrap() = 0`. Do the refuse/backoff bookkeeping under a single mutex to
  close the TOCTOU. Record `stop_scan` events in `scan_times` too.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `scan_burst_is_throttled_within_window` (which only covers the
  first refusal, never the reset or the second escalation).

#### BLE-18: The service UUID is used as the data characteristic UUID
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:828` (send), `:774` (poller filter)
- **What:** Both directions of the data path use `IRIS_SERVICE_UUID` where a characteristic UUID
  belongs. There is a dedicated `IRIS_IDENTIFY_CHARACTERISTIC` constant (:65-66) but no data
  characteristic constant at all.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
828          let char_uuid = IRIS_SERVICE_UUID; // IRIS control characteristic
829          for frame in &frames {
830              if let Err(e) = adapter.gatt_write(handle, char_uuid, frame.clone()) {
```
```rust
773                      // Reject frames addressed to another characteristic.
774                      if w.char_uuid != IRIS_SERVICE_UUID { continue; }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** In GATT a service UUID and a characteristic UUID live in different namespaces
  and must be distinct; `BluetoothGatt.getService(uuid).getCharacteristic(uuid)` with the same UUID
  resolves nothing. The trailing comment at :828 ("IRIS control characteristic") shows the author knew
  a separate characteristic was intended.
- **Root cause:** The constant was never defined, and the simulator's `gatt_write` (ble.rs:303-318)
  records whatever UUID it is handed without validating it, so tests pass.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Any write on a real device: the Kotlin adapter looks up the
  characteristic by the service UUID inside the IRIS service and gets `null`.
- **Impact:** No data ever traverses a real GATT link. Note `SimulatedBleAdapter::gatt_read`
  (ble.rs:319-327) *does* enforce the distinction, which is why the identify path works and the data
  path does not — the asymmetry is a strong tell.
- **Fix:** Add `pub const IRIS_DATA_CHARACTERISTIC: Uuid = Uuid([3, 0, ...]);` and use it in both
  places. Add it to the GATT server definition on both platforms.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `gatt_write_flows_into_incoming` and every poller test injects
  `Uuid::from_u128(1)` (== `IRIS_SERVICE_UUID`) and must be re-pointed; both platform GATT server
  implementations.

#### BLE-19: BLE `discover_peers` ignores `DiscoveryConfig::filter` and `::timeout`
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:533-627`; contrast `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:891-895`
- **What:** Only `config.max_peers` is read. `config.filter` and `config.timeout` are never touched.
- **Evidence** — Wi-Fi Aware honours the filter:
```rust
891              if let Some(filter) = config.filter.as_ref() {
892                  if !filter.contains(&peer_id) { continue; }
893              }
```
  In ble.rs, `grep -n "config\." ble.rs` yields only `config.max_peers` (:563, :565).
- **Why it is wrong:** `DiscoveryConfig` (message.rs:152-159) documents `filter` as "Only report these
  peers (None = all)" and `timeout` as "How long to scan before reporting `DiscoveryTimeout`". BLE
  silently returns unfiltered results and can never produce `TransportError::DiscoveryTimeout`, which
  exists in error.rs:14 for exactly this.
- **Root cause:** BLE `discover_peers` returns a snapshot of already-drained results rather than a
  live scan stream, so a timeout has nothing to bound and the filter step was simply never added.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** The engine calls `discover_peers` with `filter: Some(vec![target])`
  expecting one peer; it gets every IRIS beacon in range and must filter downstream, or (worse) trusts
  the contract and connects to the wrong candidate.
- **Impact:** Contract divergence between transports behind a shared trait — code written against the
  Wi-Fi Aware behaviour misbehaves on BLE. Wasted discovery work in dense environments.
- **Fix:** Add the same `config.filter` check to the `filter_map` at :583, and either implement the
  timeout (drive a real scan window) or return `DiscoveryTimeout` when the drain is empty after
  `config.timeout`. Also apply the filter *before* the iOS probe branch so the probe budget is not
  spent on peers the caller does not want.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `mod.rs` `Transport` trait docs, `manager.rs`; add a
  filter-honoured BLE test (none exists).

#### BLE-20: `CapabilityBits::set` in `ble_advert` does not mask reserved bits — the builder can emit a beacon its own parser rejects
- **Severity:** Low
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble_advert.rs:58-60`; contrast `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware_beacon.rs:63-65`
- **What:** The BLE variant ORs the raw argument in; the Wi-Fi Aware variant masks it to the known set.
- **Evidence** — ble_advert.rs:
```rust
 58      pub fn set(&mut self, bit: u16) {
 59          self.0 |= bit;
 60      }
```
  wifiaware_beacon.rs:
```rust
 63      pub fn set(&mut self, bit: u16) {
 64          self.0 |= bit & Self::all().bits();
 65      }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `parse` at ble_advert.rs:124-126 rejects any bit outside `0b11111` with
  `ReservedBits`. `set` can produce exactly such a value, so `build(caps, ..)` followed by `parse` can
  round-trip-fail — an invariant violation the type was created to prevent. `from_bits` (:52-54)
  masks correctly; `set` is the odd one out.
- **Root cause:** The two beacon modules are near-duplicates written at different times; the masking
  fix landed in one and not the other.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A future capability bit (say `bit 5`) is added to the constant list
  but the mask in `all()` is not updated. `start_advertising` (ble.rs:647-652) calls `caps.set(...)`,
  builds the beacon, and every peer rejects it with `ReservedBits` — the node becomes undiscoverable
  and the only symptom is a parse error on the far side.
- **Impact:** A latent forward-compatibility footgun that turns a one-line capability addition into a
  silent network partition.
- **Fix:** `self.0 |= bit & Self::all().bits();` — make it identical to the Wi-Fi Aware version. Add a
  property test: for all `u16` inputs, `parse(build(set_all(x), ..))` succeeds.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `ble.rs:647-652` (the only production caller); `reserved_bits_rejected`.

#### BLE-21: `MAX_ADVERT_BYTES` is unwired — `DiscoveryBeacon::parse` has no upper bound
- **Severity:** Low
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble_advert.rs:151-152` (const), `:115-139` (fn `parse`); contrast `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware_beacon.rs:128-130`
- **What:** The constant exists and is documented as "Maximum bytes of advertised payload IRIS will
  scan/accept", but `parse` never checks it. The Wi-Fi Aware twin does.
- **Evidence** — grep:
```
$ grep -rn "MAX_ADVERT_BYTES" crates/ --include=*.rs
ble_advert.rs:152:pub const MAX_ADVERT_BYTES: usize = 512;
ble_advert.rs:223:        assert_eq!(padded.len(), MAX_ADVERT_BYTES);   <- test scaffolding only
```
  wifiaware_beacon.rs enforces its equivalent:
```rust
128          if bytes.len() > MAX_SERVICE_SPECIFIC_INFO_BYTES {
129              return Err(BeaconError::TooLong);
130          }
```
  `AdvertError` (ble_advert.rs:66-77) has no `TooLong` variant at all.
- **Why it is wrong:** ble_advert.rs:10-12 promises *"malformed/truncated/oversized adverts must be
  rejected without panic or allocation blowup"*. Oversized is not rejected. BLE 5 Extended Advertising
  carries up to 1650 bytes across chained PDUs, above the 512-byte constant.
- **Root cause:** The constant was added for documentation and the test's padding assertion, then
  never wired into the parser; `AdvertError` was never given the matching variant.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A hostile Extended-Advertising broadcaster emits 1650-byte adverts.
  Each one is accepted (only the 22-byte prefix is read) and copied into a `ScanResult.payload` `Vec`
  by the bridge. At `max_peers = 64` that is ~105 KB per discovery pass, all from one attacker.
- **Impact:** Modest memory amplification and a stated defensive bound that does not exist. Low
  severity because the prefix parse itself is safe.
- **Fix:** Add `AdvertError::TooLong` and check `bytes.len() > MAX_ADVERT_BYTES` at the top of `parse`,
  mirroring wifiaware_beacon.rs:128-130. Extend `all_len_2_to_22_rejected_no_panic` with an oversize case.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `ble.rs:600`, `:604` (both `parse` call sites use `.ok()`, so a new
  error variant needs no signature change); `oversized_payload_tolerated_without_panic`.

#### BLE-22: Beacon `freshness_minutes` and `capabilities` are parsed and then thrown away
- **Severity:** Low
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble_advert.rs:92-93`, `wifiaware_beacon.rs:100-101`; consumers `ble.rs:604-624`, `wifiaware.rs:887-901`
- **What:** Both beacons carry an anti-stale freshness field and a capability bitmask. Neither
  transport reads either one after parsing — the only thing extracted is `candidate_peer_id()`.
- **Evidence:** `grep -rn "freshness_minutes\|capabilities.contains" crates/ --include=*.rs` returns
  only definitions, `build`, `parse`, and assertions inside the two beacon modules' own tests. In
  ble.rs:619-624 and wifiaware.rs:896-901 the `PeerInfo` is constructed from `candidate_peer_id()`
  alone; the parsed `beacon.capabilities` and `beacon.freshness_minutes` bindings are dropped.
- **Why it is wrong:** The field is documented as an "anti-stale hint" (ble_advert.rs:92) and the
  capability bits are described as mirroring "`TransportCapabilities`-relevant features"
  (ble_advert.rs:35). Neither purpose is realised. The 4 bytes are pure overhead in a payload the
  module docs call "deliberately tiny".
- **Root cause:** The wire format was designed ahead of the consumers, and the consumers were never
  written.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A cached/replayed advert from hours ago (Android caches scan results;
  `PublishConfig::cached = true` is the Wi-Fi Aware default at wifiaware.rs:143) produces a candidate
  peer indistinguishable from a live one. `connect()` then dials a MAC that rotated away 45 minutes
  ago, burning a 30 s GATT timeout — which, per BLE-2 and BLE-3, blocks all sends and evicts the transport
  from routing.
- **Impact:** Stale-peer connect storms, and no way to skip a peer that advertises it cannot do
  `GATT_UNICAST` / `NDP_UNICAST`. Note the freshness source itself is `SystemTime` (ble.rs:657-661)
  with `unwrap_or_default()` — a device with a wrong clock emits a wrong value, so any future consumer
  must treat it as advisory.
- **Fix:** Either consume the fields (reject candidates older than N minutes modulo the u16 wrap; skip
  peers lacking the unicast capability bit) or delete them from the wire format and reclaim the bytes.
  If kept, add the wrap-around handling explicitly — `freshness` is `minutes mod 2^16` ≈ 45.5 days.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** Beacon wire format (both), `BEACON_LEN`/`WIFI_AWARE_BEACON_LEN`,
  every beacon test.

#### BLE-23: Reassembly has no aggregate byte cap and no per-chunk length validation
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** High
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble_att.rs:230-249` (fn `decode_frame`), `:284-331` (fn `push`)
- **What:** `decode_frame` validates `total`, `count` and `idx`, but never validates the *data* length
  against anything. `push` accumulates chunks with no running byte total, so the mismatch is only
  caught after the entire message has been buffered.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
238      if total > MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES { return Err(FrameError::MessageTooLarge); }
241      if count > MAX_CHUNKS { return Err(FrameError::ChunkCountTooLarge); }
244      if idx >= count { return Err(FrameError::BadChunkIndex); }
247      let data = &frame[FRAME_HEADER..];          // length never checked against `total`
248      Ok((total, msg_id, idx, count, data))
```
```rust
314          if partial.chunks[idx].is_none() {
315              partial.chunks[idx] = Some(data.to_vec());   // no running byte accounting
316              partial.received += 1;
317          }
318          if partial.received == partial.count {
320              let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(partial.total);
321              for chunk in partial.chunks { out.extend_from_slice(&chunk.expect(...)); }
324              if out.len() != partial.total { return Err(FrameError::Truncated); }   // too late
```
- **Why it is wrong:** The module header (ble_att.rs:16-19) claims *"a per-message chunk budget bounds
  memory. No allocation blowup on malformed input."* The chunk *count* is bounded; the chunk *bytes*
  are not. Worst case per `Reassembler`: `MAX_PARTIALS(64) × MAX_CHUNKS(255) × 512 B ≈ 8.36 MB`, and
  there is one `Reassembler` per connected peer (created in the poller at ble.rs:745), so nothing
  bounds the aggregate across peers.
- **Root cause:** The bound was expressed in the units that were easy to check (count) rather than the
  units that matter (bytes). The `total` field was treated as trustworthy for `Vec::with_capacity` but
  never cross-checked against arriving data.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A connected peer sends, for each of 64 distinct `msg_id`s, chunk 0
  declaring `total = 65535, count = 255` with 512 bytes of data, then never sends the rest. 8.36 MB is
  held for the full 30 s TTL. Repeat across the ~7 concurrent GATT links Android allows: ~58 MB, on a
  device the project targets at low-end Android. The declared `total` also drives
  `Vec::with_capacity(partial.total)` at :320 — a 64 KB speculative allocation per completing message
  regardless of real size.
- **Impact:** Memory-pressure DoS from any connected peer, well within a phone's OOM-killer range.
  Requires an established GATT link, which is why this is Medium rather than High.
- **Fix:** Track bytes, reject early, and cap globally:
```rust
struct Partial { total: usize, count: usize, bytes: usize, /* ... */ }
// in push, before insert:
if data.len() > total { return Err(FrameError::Truncated); }
partial.bytes += data.len();
if partial.bytes > partial.total { return Err(FrameError::Truncated); }   // fail on frame N, not at the end
```
  and use `Vec::with_capacity(partial.total.min(actual_bytes))` at :320. Consider a
  `MAX_REASSEMBLY_BYTES` budget shared across all peers.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `Reassembler::push` call site (ble.rs:777), `MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES`
  (also `caps.max_message_size` at ble.rs:384). Re-verify `partials_bounded`,
  `oversized_declared_total_rejected`, `multi_chunk_round_trip_orders_out_of_order`.


#### BLE-25: One shared `msg_id` counter for all peers, `Relaxed`, with silent wrap
- **Severity:** Low
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** High
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble_att.rs:146-148` (fn `alloc_msg_id`), `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:358` (single shared `segmenter`)
- **What:** `BleTransport` holds one `AttSegmenter`, so a single `AtomicU16` allocates message ids
  across every peer, wrapping every 65,536 messages with no detection.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
146      fn alloc_msg_id(&self) -> u16 {
147          self.next_msg.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)
148      }
```
```rust
357      /// Live ATT MTU (negotiate-late; segmenter resizes on `on_mtu_changed`).
358      segmenter: AttSegmenter,
```
- **Why it is wrong:** The counter is shared but the id space is per-peer (each poller owns its own
  `Reassembler`), so peers burn through the shared space N× faster than necessary. On wrap, the
  reassembler's collision handling (ble_att.rs:304-313) resets the partial when `count`/`total` differ
  — but a wrapped id that happens to match on *both* fields merges two unrelated messages into one
  buffer, and `out.len() == total` will then pass, delivering a corrupted payload.
- **Root cause:** `alloc_msg_id` lives on `AttSegmenter`, which was originally per-connection; the
  transport hoisted it to a single shared field.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A long-lived node exchanging 30 KB messages at MTU 23 emits ~2500
  frames per message; 65,536 message ids are consumed after ~65 k messages. Two same-shape messages
  (same `count`, same `total`) 65,536 ids apart, both in flight to the same peer within the 30 s TTL,
  silently interleave their chunks.
- **Impact:** Rare but silent payload corruption that survives reassembly's own length check. The
  envelope layer should catch it (authentication failure), so the practical impact is an unexplained
  message drop rather than corruption — but it will be extremely hard to diagnose.
- **Fix:** Move `alloc_msg_id` per-connection (store it alongside the MTU in `connections`), and add a
  monotonic-generation byte or an explicit collision check on the receive side. `Relaxed` is
  acceptable for a pure counter, but the sharing is not.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `segment_for_mtu` (ble_att.rs:172), `connections` tuple shape,
  `rt003_frames_sized_to_each_peer_own_mtu`.

#### BLE-26: `ScanFilter::rssi_threshold` is never set and `ScanResult::rssi` is never read
- **Severity:** Low
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:74-77` (`ScanFilter`), `:127-134` (`ScanResult`), `:543-553` (the only filter construction)
- **What:** Both RSSI fields are plumbed all the way through the FFI and then ignored by the transport.
- **Evidence** — the only two `ScanFilter` constructions leave the threshold defaulted:
```rust
547              ScanFilter { service_uuids: vec![IRIS_SERVICE_UUID], ..ScanFilter::default() }
552              ScanFilter::default()
```
  and `r.rssi` is never read in the `filter_map` at :583-625. The bridge substitutes a hard-coded
  floor: `rssi_floor: filter.rssi_threshold.unwrap_or(-95)` (`iris-android/src/bridge.rs:142`).
- **Why it is wrong:** RSSI is the only proximity signal BLE offers and the transport's own capability
  block advertises `range_m_min: 1 / range_m_max: 100 / range_m_typical: 10` (ble.rs:387-389) — values
  it has no way to act on. The effective floor is a magic number buried in the Android bridge, not a
  core policy, and iOS gets whatever its own bridge chose.
- **Root cause:** The domain types were modelled from the platform API surface before any consumer
  needed them.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** In a dense environment every advert at -100 dBm (effectively
  unreachable) becomes a candidate `PeerInfo` competing for the `max_peers` budget against nearby
  peers (compounding BLE-13). `connect()` then dials peers that cannot sustain a link.
- **Impact:** Wasted connect attempts, no proximity-based ranking, and a policy constant that differs
  per platform with no single source of truth.
- **Fix:** Set `rssi_threshold: Some(RSSI_FLOOR_DBM)` from a core constant in both filter branches,
  and carry `rssi` into `PeerInfo` (or at least sort candidates by it before applying `max_peers`).
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `PeerInfo` (message.rs) would need an RSSI/quality field; both
  bridges; `discover_beacon_maps_to_peer_exactly`.

#### BLE-27: Wi-Fi Aware poller backlog is unbounded — the per-tick budget bounds CPU but not memory
- **Severity:** High
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed  ·  Tier 0  ·  commit 6dec4e7  ·  2026-08-26  ·  Backlog capped at 64×`MAX_FRAMES_PER_TICK`, oldest frames dropped with a warning log once full. `cargo test --workspace` green. **PENDING HARDWARE VERIFICATION** (needs a real adapter producing a sustained burst to confirm the bound actually engages).
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:754-799` (fn `spawn_poller`)
- **What:** Every tick the poller appends the adapter's entire batch to a `VecDeque` and forwards at
  most `MAX_FRAMES_PER_TICK` (8). If the adapter returns more than 8 per tick, the deque grows forever.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
755              let mut backlog: std::collections::VecDeque<IncomingNdpData> =
756                  std::collections::VecDeque::new();
757              loop {
760                  let fast = !links.lock().unwrap().is_empty();
761                  tokio::time::sleep(Duration::from_millis(if fast { 10 } else { IDLE_POLL_MS })).await;
765                  backlog.extend(adapter.incoming_ndp().await);      // unbounded growth
766                  for _ in 0..MAX_FRAMES_PER_TICK {
767                      let Some(frame) = backlog.pop_front() else { break; };
```
- **Why it is wrong:** The doc comment at :737-744 claims *"a bounded per-tick budget caps churn…
  so a real adapter returning a large batch can never cause unbounded per-tick work… Overflow beyond
  the budget is buffered in a local backlog"*. Both halves are true and together they are the bug: the
  work is bounded by moving the unboundedness into memory. The *simulator* cannot expose it, because
  `SimMeshCoordinator::MAX_DRAIN_PER_CALL` is deliberately pinned equal to `MAX_FRAMES_PER_TICK`
  (:278-284) — so in tests, drain ≤ forward, always. A real adapter has no such constraint;
  `WifiAwareBridge::incoming_ndp` (`iris-android/src/bridge.rs:309-324`) forwards whatever Kotlin returns.
- **Root cause:** The NEW-WA-RT-105 fix ("no frame loss") and the WAW-RT-005 fix ("bounded per-tick
  work") were satisfied simultaneously by adding an unbounded buffer between them. The sim's
  self-imposed drain cap made the residual risk invisible.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** The transport advertises `typical_throughput_bps: 20_000_000`
  (:534) and `max_message_size: 1 MiB` (:527, :62). At 20 Mbps with 1 KB frames the radio delivers
  ~2500 frames/s; the poller forwards 800/s (8 per 10 ms). Net growth ≈ 1700 frames/s. With 1 MiB
  frames the growth is measured in gigabytes per second.
- **Impact:** OOM-kill of the app under exactly the sustained throughput Wi-Fi Aware exists to provide.
  Not adversarial — an honest fast peer triggers it.
- **Fix:** Bound the backlog and account the loss:
```rust
const MAX_BACKLOG_FRAMES: usize = 256;
for f in adapter.incoming_ndp().await {
    if backlog.len() >= MAX_BACKLOG_FRAMES { dropped_inbound.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); continue; }
    backlog.push_back(f);
}
```
  and raise `MAX_FRAMES_PER_TICK` (or shorten the tick) so steady-state drain ≥ steady-state arrival.
  Better still: replace polling with an adapter-push `mpsc` channel of fixed capacity so backpressure
  reaches the platform.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `SimMeshCoordinator::MAX_DRAIN_PER_CALL` (whose equality assumption
  should be documented as sim-only), `INCOMING_CHANNEL_CAPACITY`, `dropped_inbound` (BLE-33). Add a
  test with an adapter returning 100 frames per call.

#### BLE-28: The availability watcher never runs on real hardware — `Degraded` is a simulator-only state
- **Severity:** High
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed  ·  Tier 0  ·  commit 395fb03  ·  2026-08-26  ·  Same fix as FFI-16 below (they are the same underlying defect, filed by two different reviewers): the bridge now synthesizes `availability_stream()` by polling `is_available()`. **PENDING HARDWARE VERIFICATION.**
- **Confidence:** High
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:199-201` (default `availability_stream`), `:810-853` (fn `spawn_avail_watcher`)
- **What:** `availability_stream()` has a default returning `None`; `spawn_avail_watcher` silently
  returns when it gets `None`; and `WifiAwareBridge` — the only production adapter — does not override it.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
199      fn availability_stream(&self) -> Option<Pin<Box<dyn Stream<Item = bool> + Send + 'static>>> {
200          None
201      }
```
```rust
815          let Some(stream) = adapter.availability_stream() else {
816              return;                        // no log, no counter, no state change
817          };
```
  and `grep -rn "availability_stream" crates/` shows **no** hit in `iris-android/src/bridge.rs` — the
  Android FFI trait only has `fn is_available(&self) -> bool`
  (`iris-android/src/ffi/wifi_aware_adapter.rs:68-69`, whose own comment concedes "the real trait's…
  push channel become an FFI query — recorded spike finding proj-WA-1").
- **Why it is wrong:** The doc at :195-198 says *"A real adapter SHOULD override this so the transport
  can surface `Degraded` on display-off / radio-share without waiting on the poller."* The real
  adapter does not, and nothing polls `is_available()` either — grep shows `is_available()` is called
  only at decision points (`start_advertising`:921, `connect`:967/995, `send`:1024,
  `teardown_link`:676), never on a timer. So on a device, the transport's state changes only when
  something else happens to call one of those.
- **Root cause:** A `SHOULD` in a doc comment with a permissive default and a silent `else` branch.
  The FFI projection could not express a stream, so the capability was dropped rather than replaced
  with a polled equivalent.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Display turns off; Android drops the Wi-Fi Aware data scope. No
  event fires. `state` stays `Connected` (score 40, the best available). Every `send()` hits the
  `!adapter.is_available()` guard at :1024 and returns `NotSupported` — but the *state* the manager
  selects on never changes, so the manager keeps choosing Wi-Fi Aware and every message fails.
- **Impact:** Wi-Fi Aware becomes a black hole whenever the screen is off — the dominant condition for
  a background mesh. `NEW-WA-RT-104`'s "never lie Available to the manager" guarantee holds only in
  the simulator.
- **Fix:** (a) Poll `is_available()` inside the existing poller loop (it already ticks every 10/500 ms)
  and drive `store_state_with_event` from it — this needs no FFI change. (b) Make the missing stream
  loud: `tracing::warn!` at :815 instead of a bare `return`. (c) Longer term, add an availability
  callback to `FfiWifiAwareAdapter` fed by `ACTION_WIFI_AWARE_STATE_CHANGED`.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `iris-android/src/ffi/wifi_aware_adapter.rs`,
  `iris-android/src/bridge.rs`, Kotlin adapter. Re-verify `last_link_death_while_unavailable_is_degraded`,
  `connect_while_unavailable_is_not_supported`, `availability_churn_keeps_discovery_up` (all sim-only today).

#### BLE-29: Link death is classified by substring-matching the adapter's error text
- **Severity:** High
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED (with a better false-negative than R1 supplied). See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (partial)  ·  Tier 0  ·  commit 395fb03  ·  2026-08-26  ·  Widened `is_link_loss_error` to include the real Android error strings (`"NDP terminated"`, `"NETWORK_LOST"`). **Not done:** the typed-FFI-error redesign the finding also recommends — needs a Kotlin adapter change to construct the typed variant, which cannot be verified without a build toolchain. A bare numeric failure code remains unclassifiable by string matching regardless. `cargo test -p iris-core --lib` green. **PENDING HARDWARE VERIFICATION.**
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:583-594` (fn `is_link_loss_error`), used at `:1045`
- **What:** Whether an NDP is torn down or kept depends on whether the platform's error *string*
  contains one of five English substrings.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
587  fn is_link_loss_error(e: &str) -> bool {
588      let e = e.to_ascii_lowercase();
589      e.contains("not open")
590          || e.contains("closed")
591          || e.contains("disconnect")
592          || e.contains("reset")
593          || e.contains("link lost")
594  }
```
  and the error arrives as an opaque `String` because the trait says so (`wifiaware.rs:182`:
  `async fn ndp_send(&self, ndp: NdpHandle, payload: &[u8]) -> Result<(), String>`), stringified by
  the bridge: `.map_err(|e| e.to_string())` (`iris-android/src/bridge.rs:302-307`).
- **Why it is wrong:** This is the single most consequential decision in the adapter — tear down a
  link or keep routing into it — and it is made by parsing a diagnostic string produced by a Kotlin
  layer under no obligation to keep any particular wording. It fails in both directions:
  * **False negative:** Android's `WifiAwareNetworkSpecifier` failures surface as `"NDP terminated"`,
    `"NETWORK_LOST"`, or a bare numeric code. None match. The link is treated as transient congestion
    forever; every send returns `Busy`; `teardown_link` never runs; the peer stays `Connected`.
  * **False positive:** `"connection reset by peer"` from a transient buffer condition, or `"socket
    closed"` during a benign re-key, matches → an alive link is torn down → reconnect storm, the very
    thing NEW-WA-RT-107 was written to prevent.
  A localised or vendor-modified Android build breaks the matching entirely.
- **Root cause:** `Result<(), String>` on the trait. There is no error *type* to match on, so the
  classifier had no choice but to inspect prose. The FFI has a real error enum
  (`IrisFfiError`) that is flattened to a string at the bridge.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Peer walks out of range mid-transfer. Kotlin reports
  `"android.net.wifi.aware: NDP terminated (reason 3)"`. No substring matches → `TransportError::Busy`
  → link kept → state stays `Connected` (score 40) → the router keeps selecting a dead path.
- **Impact:** The primary link-loss detection mechanism for Wi-Fi Aware is unreliable on the only
  platform that implements it. Combined with BLE-28 (no availability push), Wi-Fi Aware has **no
  dependable disconnect detection at all**.
- **Fix:** Replace the `String` error with a typed enum on the trait:
```rust
pub enum NdpError { LinkLost, Congested, NotOpen, Other(String) }
async fn ndp_send(&self, ndp: NdpHandle, payload: &[u8]) -> Result<(), NdpError>;
```
  Map `IrisFfiError` variants to it in the bridge; keep the substring matcher only as a fallback for
  `Other`, behind a `tracing::warn!` so unclassified errors are visible.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `WifiAwareAdapter` trait (all 12 ops use `Result<_, String>`),
  `SimulatedWifiAwareAdapter`, `FlakyAdapter` (test), `iris-android/src/bridge.rs`,
  `iris-android/src/ffi/wifi_aware_adapter.rs`. Re-verify `transient_send_error_keeps_link`.

#### BLE-30: The two hot-path drains are infallible by signature, forcing every adapter error to be swallowed
- **Severity:** High
- **Verdict:** CONFIRMED. See §14.
- **Fix status:** ✅ Fixed (partial)  ·  Tier 0  ·  commit 395fb03  ·  2026-08-26  ·  `WifiAwareAdapter::matches`/`incoming_ndp` are now fallible end-to-end (trait, simulated adapter, Android bridge, both callers). **Not done:** the identical pattern on BLE's `incoming_gatt_writes()`/`scan_results()` — structurally different (sync, `MutexGuard`-returning, not async `Vec`-returning), needs its own design. `cargo test --workspace` green. **PENDING HARDWARE VERIFICATION.**
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:172-173` (`matches`), `:184-185` (`incoming_ndp`); same defect at `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:175`, `:177`
- **What:** `matches()` and `incoming_ndp()` return bare `Vec`s. The FFI beneath them is fallible, so
  the bridge has to discard the error.
- **Evidence** — the core trait:
```rust
172      /// Drain current discovery matches.
173      async fn matches(&self) -> Vec<PeerDiscovery>;
184      /// Drain inbound NDP frames.
185      async fn incoming_ndp(&self) -> Vec<IncomingNdpData>;
```
  the FFI is fallible (`iris-android/src/ffi/wifi_aware_adapter.rs:62,66`):
```rust
    async fn matches(&self) -> Result<Vec<FfiPeerDiscovery>, IrisFfiError>;
    async fn incoming_ndp(&self) -> Result<Vec<FfiIncomingNdpData>, IrisFfiError>;
```
  so the bridge must throw the error away (`iris-android/src/bridge.rs`):
```rust
    async fn matches(&self) -> Vec<WaPeerDiscovery> {
        self.ffi.matches().await.unwrap_or_default()   // session died == no peers
    }
    async fn incoming_ndp(&self) -> Vec<IncomingNdpData> {
        self.ffi.incoming_ndp().await.unwrap_or_default()
    }
```
- **Why it is wrong:** These are the two operations that carry all inbound information. A NAN session
  that has been torn down by the framework, a revoked `NEARBY_WIFI_DEVICES` permission, or a
  `WifiAwareSession` that threw `IllegalStateException` all present to the core as "zero peers, zero
  frames" — indistinguishable from a quiet radio. `discover_peers` returns `Ok(empty stream)` and the
  poller loops forever on an empty drain.
- **Root cause:** The trait was shaped after `SimulatedWifiAwareAdapter`, whose drains genuinely cannot
  fail. The same mistake appears in `BleAdapter`, where the drains return `MutexGuard` (also infallible
  — and see BLE-4 for the second problem that shape causes).
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** User revokes the nearby-devices permission while the app runs. Every
  `matches()` throws in Kotlin; `unwrap_or_default()` yields `[]`; the transport reports `Available`
  with no peers, forever. Nothing prompts the user, nothing logs, nothing retries differently.
- **Impact:** Permanent silent failure of the entire Wi-Fi Aware transport, presenting as "no peers
  nearby". Identically for BLE's `scan_results()`/`incoming_gatt_writes()`.
- **Fix:** Make the drains fallible: `async fn matches(&self) -> Result<Vec<PeerDiscovery>, NdpError>`
  and likewise for `incoming_ndp`. In the poller, count consecutive failures and drive
  `set_state(Unavailable)` past a threshold. Apply the same change to `BleAdapter`'s two drains
  (which BLE-4 requires reshaping anyway).
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `WifiAwareAdapter` and `BleAdapter` traits and every implementor
  (sim + 5 test adapters in ble.rs, sim + `FlakyAdapter` in wifiaware.rs), both bridges.
  Re-verify `discovery_finds_advertising_peer`, `ndp_roundtrip_delivers_payload`.

#### BLE-31: `IncomingNdpData::ndp` is never resolved — real adapters attribute every frame to `PeerId([0;32])`
- **Severity:** Low  *(as filed: High — corrected by adversarial verification)*
- **Verdict:** PARTIALLY-CORRECT (core factual assertion refuted; residual gap real but minor). See §14.
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** High
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:114-121` (struct), `:779-784` (attribution)
- **What:** The struct carries a local NDP handle specifically so the receiver can map a frame to a
  peer, but the transport never looks it up in `links`. Only the optional `sender` field is used.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
779                      // NEW-WA-RT-101: prefer the adapter-reported sender candidate
780                      // (sim) / underlying NDP peer mapping (real adapter resolves
781                      // `frame.ndp` itself). Best-effort only ...
784                      let peer_id = frame.sender.unwrap_or(PeerId([0u8; 32]));
```
  `grep -rn "\.ndp\b" crates/` shows `frame.ndp` is **never read** — the only `.ndp` accesses are
  `l.ndp` on `NdpLink` (:670, :1033, :1095, :1533) and the constructor `d.ndp.0` in the Android sim
  harness (`iris-android/src/engine.rs:428`).
- **Why it is wrong:** The comment asserts the real adapter "resolves `frame.ndp` itself", but the
  adapter cannot: `sender` is `Option<Vec<u8>>` over FFI
  (`iris-android/src/ffi/wifi_aware_adapter.rs:43`) and a NAN peer's IRIS `PeerId` is not something
  the Kotlin layer knows — the beacon→PeerId mapping lives entirely in Rust
  (`WifiAwareBeacon::candidate_peer_id`, wifiaware_beacon.rs:156-160). The `links` vector already
  holds exactly the `NdpHandle → PeerId` mapping needed, and it is right there.
- **Root cause:** NEW-WA-RT-101 was fixed by teaching the *simulator* to report `sender` (which it
  can, because the coordinator knows every peer's beacon) rather than by teaching the *transport* to
  resolve `ndp`. The comment then rationalised the gap onto the unwritten Android adapter.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Android adapter delivers a frame on NDP handle 7 with `sender: None`
  (the only thing it can honestly report). `frame.sender.unwrap_or(PeerId([0u8;32]))` → the message is
  published with an all-zero peer id, even though `links` contains `NdpLink { ndp: NdpHandle(7),
  peer_id: <the real peer> }`.
- **Impact:** On real hardware every inbound Wi-Fi Aware message is attributed to the zero peer.
  Anything keyed on sender identity — ACK routing, dedup, reputation, delivery receipts — collapses to
  a single bucket. `ndp_roundtrip_delivers_payload` asserts `assert_ne!(got.peer_id, PeerId([0u8;32]))`
  and passes only because the sim populates `sender`.
- **Fix:** Resolve the handle first, fall back to `sender`, then to zero:
```rust
let peer_id = links.lock().unwrap().iter()
    .find(|l| l.ndp == frame.ndp).map(|l| l.peer_id)
    .or(frame.sender)
    .unwrap_or(PeerId([0u8; 32]));
```
  (`links` is already cloned into the task at :752.) Keep the "candidate, not verified" caveat of BLE-8.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `NdpLink`, `teardown_link`, `iris-android/src/bridge.rs:309-324`.
  Re-verify `ndp_roundtrip_delivers_payload` — and add a variant with an adapter that reports `ndp`
  but not `sender`, which is the production shape and is currently untested.

#### BLE-32: `start_advertising` discards the node's own `PeerId` — the published beacon identity is adapter-invented
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** High
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:915-929` (fn `start_advertising`), `:363-385` (sim `beacon_bytes`/`register`); contrast `crates/iris-core/src/transport/ble.rs:653-662`
- **What:** The `NodeAdvertisement` parameter is bound to `_info` and never used. The beacon's
  `peer_short` is derived by the adapter from an internal counter tag, not from the node's real
  identity.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
915      async fn start_advertising(&self, _info: NodeAdvertisement) -> Result<(), TransportError> {
919          self.ensure_started().await?;
920          let adapter = self.adapter().await?;
924          adapter.publish(&PublishConfig::default()).await
```
  the sim invents the identity (:377-385):
```rust
377      fn register(&self) {
378          let mut tag = self.tag.lock().unwrap();
379          let mut short = [0u8; 16];
380          if *tag == 0 { *tag = self.coordinator.register_peer(vec![]); }
383          short[..8].copy_from_slice(&tag.to_le_bytes());     // identity = a counter
384          self.coordinator.set_beacon(*tag, self.beacon_bytes(&short));
```
  BLE does it correctly (ble.rs:653-654):
```rust
653          let peer_short = crate::identity::peer_id::peer_short(&info.peer_id.0);
654          let beacon = DiscoveryBeacon::build(caps, peer_short, ...);
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `PublishConfig` has no field for the beacon bytes, so there is no channel from
  the transport to the adapter for the node's `peer_short` at all. On the Android bridge,
  `publish(FfiPublishConfig { service_name, instance_id, cached, ttl_s })`
  (`iris-android/src/bridge.rs:261-269`) carries no identity either — so a real adapter cannot publish
  the node's IRIS identity even if it wanted to. Meanwhile the *receiving* side confidently parses
  `service_specific_info` into a `PeerId` (:887-890) and uses it as the peer's identity.
- **Root cause:** The publish path was built around `PublishConfig` (a NAN session-configuration
  object) rather than around the beacon, and the sim filled the identity gap with a local counter so
  round-trip tests would pass.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Any production deployment: the node publishes a beacon whose
  `peer_short` is unrelated to its `PeerId`, or (more likely) no beacon at all, so no other node can
  resolve it. In-process tests pass because both sides share one `SimMeshCoordinator` and agree on the
  invented tags.
- **Impact:** Wi-Fi Aware discovery cannot work between real devices — a peer's advertised identity
  never matches the identity it authenticates with in the envelope layer.
- **Fix:** Add the beacon bytes to the publish path, mirroring BLE:
```rust
pub struct PublishConfig { /* ... */ pub service_specific_info: Vec<u8> }
// in start_advertising:
let peer_short = crate::identity::peer_id::peer_short(&info.peer_id.0);
let ssi = WifiAwareBeacon::build(caps, peer_short, freshness_minutes());
adapter.publish(&PublishConfig { service_specific_info: ssi, ..Default::default() }).await
```
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `PublishConfig`, `FfiPublishConfig`,
  `SimulatedWifiAwareAdapter::{register, beacon_bytes}`, `iris-android/src/bridge.rs:261-269`,
  Kotlin publish. Re-verify `ndp_roundtrip_delivers_payload`, `discovery_finds_advertising_peer`,
  `availability_churn_keeps_discovery_up` (all depend on the sim's invented tags).

#### BLE-33: `dropped_inbound` is write-only — the "counted, not silently swallowed" guarantee has no reader
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:572-575` (field), `:797` (the only write)
- **What:** The counter is incremented and never read. There is no getter, no metric registration, no
  log.
- **Evidence** — the field's own doc claims telemetry:
```rust
572      /// Inbound frames that could not be delivered upstream (closed/slow
573      /// receiver), counted for telemetry instead of silently swallowed
574      /// (NEW-WA-RT-106).
575      dropped_inbound: Arc<AtomicU64>,
```
  the complete set of references:
```
$ grep -rn "dropped_inbound" crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs
575:    dropped_inbound: Arc<AtomicU64>,
630:            dropped_inbound: Arc::new(AtomicU64::new(0)),
753:        let dropped_inbound = self.dropped_inbound.clone();
797:                        dropped_inbound.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
```
  Compare `mod.rs:326-329`, which does this properly — `INBOUND_LAGGED_TOTAL` has an accessor and a
  `tracing::warn!` at the increment site.
- **Why it is wrong:** "Counted instead of silently swallowed" is only true if something can observe
  the count. A value no code can read is a swallowed error with extra steps. `wifi_direct.rs:795`
  has the identical write-only counter, so the pattern has already been copied.
- **Root cause:** NEW-WA-RT-106 was closed by adding the increment; the observability half was never
  built, and no test could catch the omission because there is nothing to assert against.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** Production inbound loss (no subscriber, or broadcast overrun). The
  counter climbs; no dashboard, log line, or debug command can show it.
- **Impact:** Undiagnosable message loss in the field, with a doc comment that actively misleads the
  next reader into thinking it is covered.
- **Fix:** Follow the `INBOUND_LAGGED_TOTAL` precedent: add
  `pub fn dropped_inbound(&self) -> u64 { self.dropped_inbound.load(Ordering::Relaxed) }`, register it
  with the observability crate, and `tracing::warn!` at the increment. Also extend it to cover the
  backlog overflow from BLE-27.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `wifi_direct.rs:795` has the same defect; the observability/metrics
  registry. Add a test asserting the counter rises when no subscriber exists.

#### BLE-34: `ensure_started` holds `connect_gate` across platform I/O and re-runs `start`+`subscribe` on every call
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:702-735` (fn `ensure_started`)
- **What:** The gate that serialises *all* connects is held across `adapter.start()` and
  `adapter.subscribe()`, and both are called on every `discover_peers` / `start_advertising`, with no
  "already started" short-circuit.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
702      async fn ensure_started(&self) -> Result<(), TransportError> {
703          let _gate = self.connect_gate.lock().await;
707          let adapter = self.adapter().await?;
708          adapter.start().await
711              .map_err(|e| TransportError::Io(format!("wifiaware.start: {e}")))?;
712          adapter.subscribe().await
715              .map_err(|e| TransportError::Io(format!("wifiaware.subscribe: {e}")))?;
716          self.spawn_poller(adapter.clone()).await?;
```
  Only `spawn_poller` (:746-749) and `spawn_avail_watcher` (:811-814) are idempotent; `start` and
  `subscribe` are unconditional.
- **Why it is wrong:** `connect_gate` is described at :563-568 as protecting the open-link critical
  section. Extending it over unrelated bring-up I/O turns every `discover_peers` into a global barrier
  for `connect()`. And the trait comments promise idempotence ("Power on the Wi-Fi Aware subsystem…
  Idempotent", :157) — a promise the *adapter* must keep because the transport re-issues the calls
  unconditionally.
- **Root cause:** NEW-WA-RT-102 needed bring-up serialised against `shutdown()`, and the simplest way
  was to take the existing gate for the whole function.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A discovery sweep calls `discover_peers`, which enters
  `ensure_started` and blocks on a slow `WifiAwareManager.attach()` (seconds on a cold radio). Every
  concurrent `connect()` blocks on `connect_gate` for that entire time, including P0 traffic.
- **Impact:** Head-of-line blocking of all NDP establishment behind unrelated discovery I/O, plus
  redundant `attach`/`subscribe` churn against the platform on every discovery pass.
- **Fix:** Add a `started: AtomicBool` and short-circuit before taking the gate; take the gate only
  around the promotion + spawn steps, not around `start`/`subscribe`. If serialisation of bring-up is
  genuinely required, use a separate `start_gate` so it does not contend with `connect`.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `connect` (:957), `shutdown` (:1085) — all three share the gate.
  Re-verify `concurrent_connects_open_single_ndp`, `connect_racing_shutdown_leaks_no_link`.

#### BLE-35: No timeout on any Wi-Fi Aware adapter call
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:708-715`, `:985-988`, `:1036`, `:924-927`, `:1094-1099`
- **What:** Every `await` on the adapter is bare. A JNI/coroutine call that never returns hangs the
  caller — and, via `connect_gate`, everything else.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
985          let ndp = adapter
986              .open_ndp(PeerHandle(handle))
987              .await
988              .map_err(|_| TransportError::ConnectionFailed)?;
```
```rust
1036          match adapter.ndp_send(ndp, &frame).await {
```
```rust
1094          if let Ok(adapter) = self.adapter().await {
1097                  let _ = adapter.close_ndp(ndp).await;
1099              let _ = adapter.shutdown().await;
```
- **Why it is wrong:** NDP establishment on Android involves a `ConnectivityManager.requestNetwork`
  round trip that can stall indefinitely when the peer is gone. `TransportError::ConnectionFailed`
  and `DiscoveryTimeout` both exist in error.rs; neither can ever be produced by a hang. Note the
  contrast with the iOS BLE leg, where the timeout is at least *claimed* to exist on the Swift side
  (`iris-ios/src/ffi/ble_adapter.rs:75-76`).
- **Root cause:** The simulator returns immediately from every op, so no test ever waits, and the
  need for deadlines never surfaced.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** `connect()` is called for a peer that just left. `open_ndp` is
  awaited at :985 while `connect_gate` is held (taken at :957). The call never resolves. Every
  subsequent `connect()` and `shutdown()` blocks on the gate forever. The transport is
  unrecoverable without a process restart.
- **Impact:** A permanent deadlock of the Wi-Fi Aware transport triggered by an ordinary,
  non-adversarial event (peer departure during connect).
- **Fix:** Wrap every adapter call in a deadline:
```rust
const NDP_OPEN_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(10);
let ndp = tokio::time::timeout(NDP_OPEN_TIMEOUT, adapter.open_ndp(PeerHandle(handle)))
    .await.map_err(|_| TransportError::ConnectionFailed)?
    .map_err(|_| TransportError::ConnectionFailed)?;
```
  Use a shorter deadline for `ndp_send` and a bounded one in `shutdown` so teardown always completes.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** All of `connect`, `send`, `shutdown`, `ensure_started`. Add a test
  with an adapter whose `open_ndp` never resolves — none exists.

#### BLE-36: `stop_discovery` is a partial stop, and `shutdown` is irreversible
- **Severity:** Medium
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:906-913` (`stop_discovery`), `:1081-1107` (`shutdown`)
- **What:** `stop_discovery` unsubscribes but leaves the poller running, the state untouched, and the
  availability watcher alive. `shutdown` latches `shutdown_flag` permanently, so the transport can
  never be restarted within the process.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
906      async fn stop_discovery(&self) -> Result<(), TransportError> {
907          let adapter = self.adapter().await?;
908          adapter.unsubscribe().await
911              .map_err(|e| TransportError::Io(format!("wifiaware.unsubscribe: {e}")))?;
912          Ok(())                       // poller still ticking, state unchanged
913      }
```
```rust
1104          self.shutdown_flag.store(true, Ordering::SeqCst);   // never cleared
1105          self.set_state(TransportState::Unavailable);
```
- **Why it is wrong:** After `stop_discovery` the transport still burns the 500 ms idle poll (or 10 ms
  if linked) forever, and still reports `Available`, so the manager keeps selecting a transport that
  is no longer discovering. And `ensure_started` (:704-706) rejects with `ShuttingDown` for the rest of
  the process, so the documented recovery story — Wi-Fi Aware drops on display-off and comes back —
  cannot be implemented via `shutdown`/restart. There is also a secondary trap: the simulator's
  `availability_stream()` uses `.take()` (:398), so it yields a stream exactly once; after `shutdown`
  aborts the watcher, no replacement watcher can ever be created even if the flag were cleared.
- **Root cause:** `shutdown_flag` was introduced for NEW-WA-RT-102 (stop a racing `ensure_started`
  from resurrecting a dead transport) and implemented as a permanent latch, conflating "shutting down
  right now" with "shut down forever".
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** The engine calls `shutdown()` on display-off to save power, then
  tries to restart on display-on. Every subsequent call returns `ShuttingDown`. Wi-Fi Aware is gone
  for the process lifetime.
- **Impact:** Wi-Fi Aware cannot be power-cycled — the app must be restarted to get it back, which is
  a non-starter for a background mesh.
- **Fix:** Make `shutdown_flag` a generation counter or an explicit `Lifecycle { Running, Stopping,
  Stopped }` that a `restart()` can move back to `Running` under `connect_gate`. Give the simulator a
  re-subscribable availability stream (`available_tx.subscribe()` instead of a one-shot `.take()`).
  In `stop_discovery`, abort the poller when no links remain and reflect the state.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `ensure_started`, `spawn_avail_watcher`,
  `SimulatedWifiAwareAdapter::availability_stream`. Re-verify `shutdown_returns_to_unavailable`,
  `connect_racing_shutdown_leaks_no_link`.

- **Severity:** Low

#### BLE-38: NAN RSSI is carried across the FFI and dropped at the bridge
- **Severity:** Low
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** Certain
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:98-103` (`PeerDiscovery`); dropped at `crates/iris-android/src/bridge.rs:376-383`
- **What:** `FfiPeerDiscovery` has an `rssi: i32` field; the core's `PeerDiscovery` has no place to put
  it, so the bridge discards it.
- **Evidence** — FFI (`iris-android/src/ffi/wifi_aware_adapter.rs:32-33`):
```rust
    /// rssi dBm.
    pub rssi: i32,
```
  core (wifiaware.rs:98-103) has only `peer_handle` and `service_specific_info`; the bridge maps
  across and silently drops the third field:
```rust
            .map(|m: FfiPeerDiscovery| WaPeerDiscovery {
                peer_handle: WaPeerHandle(m.peer_handle),
                service_specific_info: m.service_specific_info,
            })                                   // m.rssi discarded
```
- **Why it is wrong:** The platform paid to measure it and the FFI paid to marshal it, and then it is
  thrown away. `discover_peers` has no proximity signal to rank or bound candidates with — the same
  gap as BLE's BLE-26, so it is a systemic pattern rather than a one-off.
- **Root cause:** The FFI record was extended (the AC-4 projection fix noted at
  `ffi/wifi_aware_adapter.rs:28-31`) without extending the core type it mirrors.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** `config.max_peers` truncation (:886) picks candidates in adapter
  order rather than by signal strength, so a distant peer can crowd out a close one.
- **Impact:** No proximity-aware discovery; wasted `open_ndp` attempts on marginal peers.
- **Fix:** Add `pub rssi: i32` to `PeerDiscovery`, forward it in the bridge, and sort by it before the
  `take(config.max_peers)` at :886.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `SimulatedWifiAwareAdapter::matches` (:436-449), `PeerInfo` if the
  value is to reach the engine, `iris-android/src/bridge.rs`.

#### BLE-39: `connect()` trusts a caller-supplied peer handle with no cross-check against the beacon
- **Severity:** Low
- **Fix status:** ⬜ Not started  ·  Tier 4
- **Confidence:** High
- **Location:** `crates/iris-core/src/transport/wifiaware.rs:945-950`, `:999-1002`
- **What:** The NDP target is parsed out of a decimal string in `PeerInfo::transport_addresses` and
  used directly; the link is then registered under `peer.peer_id` with no verification that the handle
  and the id came from the same discovery match.
- **Evidence:**
```rust
945          let handle = peer
946              .transport_addresses
947              .iter()
948              .find(|(k, _)| k == "wifi-aware")
949              .and_then(|(_, v)| v.parse::<u64>().ok())
950              .ok_or(TransportError::PeerNotFound)?;
...
999          self.links.lock().unwrap().push(NdpLink { ndp, peer_id: peer.peer_id });
```
- **Why it is wrong:** `discover_peers` produces the `(peer_id, peer_handle)` pair atomically at
  :896-901, but `connect()` accepts any pair a caller assembles. `NdpLink` is what `send()` resolves
  against (:1027-1034) and what BLE-31's fix would use for inbound attribution, so a mismatched pair
  silently misroutes both directions. `.ok()` at :949 also collapses a malformed handle string into
  `PeerNotFound`, losing the distinction between "no wifi-aware address" and "a corrupt one".
- **Root cause:** `PeerInfo` is a plain data struct with no provenance, so the discovery→connect
  correlation is by convention only.
- **Trigger / failure scenario:** A `PeerInfo` reconstructed from persisted storage after the NAN
  session restarted: peer handles are session-scoped and get reassigned, so the stored handle now
  points at a different peer. The transport opens an NDP to peer X and files it under peer Y's id.
- **Impact:** Silent cross-peer misrouting of unicast traffic after any session restart. Low severity
  only because the envelope layer should reject the mismatch — but the transport will report success.
- **Fix:** Keep a `HashMap<PeerId, PeerHandle>` populated by `discover_peers` and validate the
  caller-supplied handle against it (or ignore the caller's value entirely and look it up). Expire
  entries on `unsubscribe`/session restart. Distinguish the two `PeerNotFound` causes.
- **Dependencies / blast radius:** `discover_peers`, `NdpLink`, `send`; would also strengthen BLE-31.
